title: Open-source tools for learning graphs (generated)
summary: A survey of open-source projects that combine prerequisite concept graphs, visual exploration, LLM agents and human curation, with the research and design lessons for building one.

concepts.title: Prerequisite model
concepts.summary: Typed, directed 'you need A before B' edges between concepts, ideally forming a validated DAG.
concepts.overview: A prerequisite model is the data structure at the heart of the whole survey: concepts as nodes, and typed, directed edges meaning 'you need A before B'. The rubric asks for more than 'related to' links. The edges must be directional and, ideally, checked to form a [directed acyclic graph](#c/c-dag), so there is always a valid reading order. This is what lets a system compute a [personalized learning plan](#c/c-learning-plan) the way [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy) did. It is also the pillar that LLM-heavy tools skip: [AI tutors](#c/c-ai-tutors) generate lessons and 'mastery paths' with no explicit, curatable [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph) behind them. And it's where LLMs are weakest, since [they are not reliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges), which is why the design advice routes these edges through human review.

sections.heading: What counts as a prerequisite model?
sections.md: The rubric asks for **typed, directed 'requires' edges**, ideally a validated DAG, and explicitly not just 'related to' links. The first pillar puts it more plainly: knowledge is split into well-defined chunks (nodes), and edges say *'you need A before B'*. A tool scores strong (●) when those edges are first-class, partial (◐) when ordering exists but is weaker (Oppia's prerequisite skills, roadmap.sh's roadmap order, Graphify's generic relations), and none (○) when the structure is a hierarchy, an outline or plain links.

sections.heading: Who has one?
sections.md: In the comparison matrix, [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy), [Learning Commons](#c/c-learning-commons-kg) (progressions and dependencies), [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint) (dependencies recorded in its uses lists), [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph), [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder) (a cycle-validated DAG), [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything) (code dependencies) and [Obsidian + Breadcrumbs](#c/c-obsidian-breadcrumbs) (typed links) all score strong. The most popular LLM tools score none: [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor), [OpenMAIC](#c/c-openmaic) (a linear outline), the [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/c-llm-wiki) (links only), [Co-STORM](#c/c-co-storm) (a hierarchy) and [GraphRAG infrastructure](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure).

sections.heading: Why is it the hard part?
sections.md: Prerequisite edges are where LLMs are weakest and where errors cost the most. On K12-Bench, frontier models reach only about 46–57% exact match on prerequisite reasoning, and a missing or backwards edge sends a learner into material they can't yet follow. Code tools get away with mechanical extraction because code dependencies can be parsed; general knowledge can't be parsed that way, so its edges have to be proposed by an LLM and verified by a person.

sections.heading: What should the edges look like?
sections.md: The design section argues for [distinct edge types](#c/c-edge-types): `requires` (a [hard prerequisite](#c/c-hard-prerequisite)), `helps` (a [soft one](#c/c-soft-prerequisite)), `part-of`, `related` and `encompasses` (Math Academy-style implicit practice). It also suggests [depth-qualified prerequisites](#c/c-depth-qualified-prerequisites), such as 'requires B at the *apply* level, not just *define*'. Each AI-made edge should be a [proposal with confidence and evidence](#c/c-edge-proposals), and a file-based graph should get [CI checks for cycles and dangling references](#c/c-ci-graph-checks) so it stays a valid DAG.

sections.heading: What would a newcomer get wrong?
sections.md: The common mistake is to treat any link as a prerequisite. 'Related to' says two ideas belong together; 'requires' says one can't be understood without the other. Mind maps and wikis are full of the first kind and have almost none of the second, which is why the survey scores tools with rich link structures, like the LLM Wiki or Co-STORM, as having no prerequisite model at all. A second mistake is to assume the graph is a tree. A concept often has several prerequisites from different branches of a subject, so a tree forces an arbitrary choice of parent and loses the rest. That's why the rubric asks for a DAG and why tree-shaped tools can't serve.

concepts.title: Chunked nodes
concepts.summary: Each node is a self-contained learning unit with an explanation, resources and checks.
concepts.overview: Chunking is the rubric's test of whether a graph's nodes are real learning units. A good node is self-contained: it carries an explanation, resources and some check of understanding, so a learner can land on it and learn from it. It's the other half of the first pillar, since a [prerequisite model](#c/c-prerequisite-model) is only useful if the things it orders are well defined. [Oppia](#c/c-oppia) is the survey's model of good granularity: a [skill](#c/c-skill-granularity) phrased as 'given X, compute Y', with worked examples and misconceptions attached. Most tools score well here, even those with no prerequisite edges; the weak scores go to [GraphRAG infrastructure](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure), whose entity nodes aren't learning units at all.

concepts.title: Visual graph exploration
concepts.summary: A learner-facing graph or map to explore, not just a list.
concepts.overview: The second pillar is visual exploration: a learner can see where a concept sits, what it depends on and what it unlocks. The rubric asks for a learner-facing graph or map, not just a list. Several strong prerequisite systems fail here, notably [Oppia](#c/c-oppia) and [Learning Commons](#c/c-learning-commons-kg), while code tools like [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything) and [Graphify](#c/c-graphify) excel. The survey's design advice is specific: prerequisite graphs are DAGs, not trees, so a [layered layout](#c/c-layered-layout) with foundations at the bottom reads far better than a [force-directed](#c/c-force-directed-layout) one. The recommended shape is [DAG-first visualization](#c/c-dag-first-visualization): a 'what do I need first?' view for one target, zoomable out to a whole-field map, with a [mastery overlay](#c/c-mastery-overlay).

sections.heading: What the pillar asks for
sections.md: A learner should be able to *see* the knowledge: where a concept sits, what it depends on, and what it unlocks. The rubric scores a tool strong only for a learner-facing graph or map exploration, not a list, a table of contents or a static diagram.

sections.heading: Who does it well, and who doesn't?
sections.md: Strong: [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint)'s rendered dependency graph, [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph)'s interactive concept map with overview-to-detail zoom, [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything)'s force-directed codebase graph, [Graphify](#c/c-graphify), [Obsidian + Breadcrumbs](#c/c-obsidian-breadcrumbs) and [roadmap.sh](#c/c-roadmap-sh). Partial: [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy), [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder), [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor) (Mermaid diagrams), the [LLM Wiki](#c/c-llm-wiki) through Obsidian, and [Co-STORM](#c/c-co-storm)'s mind map. None: [Oppia](#c/c-oppia), [Learning Commons](#c/c-learning-commons-kg) and [OpenMAIC](#c/c-openmaic). The prerequisite-graph learning systems as a group have the right data model but weak visualization.

sections.heading: Which layout?
sections.md: Prerequisite graphs are **DAGs, not trees**. Tree-shaped mind-map libraries like [markmap](#c/c-markmap) are an easy LLM output target but can't express a DAG. A [layered (Sugiyama) layout](#c/c-layered-layout), with foundations at the bottom and goals at the top, reads far better for 'what do I need first?' than the [force-directed layouts](#c/c-force-directed-layout) most graph tools default to. [React Flow](#c/c-react-flow) with [dagre or ELK](#c/c-dagre-elk) suits an editable curation view; [Cytoscape.js](#c/c-cytoscape-js) or [Sigma.js](#c/c-sigma-js) suit a learner view, Sigma when the map has thousands of nodes.

sections.heading: What the survey recommends
sections.md: Make visualization [DAG-first](#c/c-dag-first-visualization). Show a layered view of one target concept's prerequisites, like Metacademy's learning plan, zoomable out to a whole-field map at Sigma.js scale. Overlay mastery, and draw AI-proposed edges that haven't been reviewed in a distinct style, so learners and curators can tell verified structure from suggestions.

sections.heading: What makes it hard to get right?
sections.md: A graph view has to serve two readers with different needs. A learner wants a short, ordered path to one goal; a curator wants to see everything, including edges that are still only proposals. A single force-directed picture of the whole graph serves neither: it's too dense to read a path from and hides direction. That's why the survey separates an editable curation view (React Flow) from a learner view (Cytoscape.js or Sigma.js), and why it starts the learner view from one target rather than the whole field. Scale matters too: a whole-field map of thousands of concepts needs a WebGL renderer, which is what Sigma.js is for.

concepts.title: LLM / agent capabilities
concepts.summary: An LLM or agent generates structure and content, tutors, or evaluates the learner.
concepts.overview: The third pillar asks whether the tool has built-in LLM or agent capabilities: generating nodes, proposing edges, writing explanations, tutoring and checking mastery. This is where the 2026 wave of tools is strongest. [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor) and [OpenMAIC](#c/c-openmaic) generate lessons, quizzes and whole classrooms, and [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything) and [Graphify](#c/c-graphify) build graphs with agents. The classic [prerequisite-graph systems](#c/c-prerequisite-graph-learning-systems) mostly have none. The survey's point is that LLM power alone isn't enough: [LLMs are unreliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges), so their output should arrive as [proposals](#c/c-edge-proposals) that a human reviews, and mastery should come from a transparent model rather than LLM judgment.

sections.heading: What the pillar covers
sections.md: The survey lists five jobs for the model: generate nodes, propose edges, write explanations, tutor, and check mastery. The rubric scores a tool strong if an LLM generates or suggests structure or content, tutors, or evaluates.

sections.heading: Where the LLM power is today
sections.md: The [AI tutors and course generators](#c/c-ai-tutors) have huge 2026 adoption. [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor) (~40k★) offers RAG over your materials, tutoring, quiz generation and 'mastery paths'; [OpenMAIC](#c/c-openmaic) (~39k★) turns a document into a multi-agent classroom. The [graphs-that-teach tools for code](#c/c-graphs-that-teach-code) use multi-agent pipelines to build graphs and guided tours. [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph) and [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder) combine agents with a real prerequisite DAG, but they are tiny (0–1★). [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy), [Oppia](#c/c-oppia) and [roadmap.sh](#c/c-roadmap-sh)'s open repo have no LLM at all.

sections.heading: Where the LLM should not have the last word
sections.md: On K12-Bench, frontier LLMs score only ~46–57% exact match on prerequisite reasoning, so the survey concludes that [LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges). Two design rules follow. Every AI-made edge is a [proposal with confidence and cited evidence](#c/c-edge-proposals), routed to a [human review queue](#c/c-review-queue) when it's uncertain or high-impact. And mastery should come from a [transparent model](#c/c-claim-transparent-mastery) such as [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/c-bkt), not from asking an LLM.

sections.heading: How to split the work between agents
sections.md: The [suggested starting stack](#c/c-starting-stack) names three agents: a [proposer](#c/c-proposer-agent) that extracts concepts and edges from sources with citations, a [critic](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent) that checks for cycles, finds missing prerequisites and verifies evidence, and a [tutor](#c/c-tutor-agent) that writes per-node explanations and quizzes. That matches the survey's advice to [keep the graph separate from the tutor](#c/c-separate-graph-from-tutor): the curated DAG decides *what* to learn, the LLM handles *how*.

sections.heading: What does 'agent' add over a single LLM call?
sections.md: Several of the strongest tools split the work across specialized agents rather than one prompt. Understand-Anything runs a scanner, file and architecture analyzers, a tour-builder and a graph-reviewer. PathFinder uses LangGraph agents for gap finding, scheduling, and quiz and explanation generation. OpenMAIC casts agents as a teacher, a TA and classmates. The benefit for a learning graph is separation of concerns: the agent that proposes an edge isn't the one that checks it, which is why an independent critic or reviewer appears in both SyllabusGraph and Understand-Anything and in the suggested stack.

concepts.title: Human + LLM co-curation
concepts.summary: A person reviews, edits and approves what the LLM proposes, with provenance and versioning.
concepts.overview: The fourth pillar is human and LLM co-curation: a person reviews, edits and approves what the model proposes, and the system records provenance. The rubric looks for a review or approval workflow, direct editing, provenance and versioning. It matters because LLM-made prerequisite edges are wrong often enough to hurt learners, and because the older alternative, experts hand-writing everything, hit a [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck). The survey's models are [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint) (humans and AI working in parallel on small nodes), [ACE](#c/c-ace) (experts confirm only top-ranked candidate edges) and [plain files plus git](#c/c-files-plus-git), where agents and humans edit the same files and review happens in diffs. The proposed product centres on a [review queue](#c/c-review-queue) for AI-proposed edges.

sections.heading: What co-curation means here
sections.md: A person reviews, edits and approves what the LLM proposes, **with provenance**. The rubric scores review and approve workflows, direct editing, provenance and versioning. It's the pillar that turns an LLM's guesses into a graph a learner can trust.

sections.heading: Why it's needed
sections.md: Two failures bracket the problem. Hand curation alone doesn't scale: [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy)'s downfall was the [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck), with experts hand-writing every node and edge. LLMs alone aren't accurate enough: frontier models reach only ~46–57% exact match on K12-Bench prerequisite reasoning. Research like [ACE](#c/c-ace) shows the middle path works: ranking candidate edges and asking experts to confirm only the top ones cut expert effort a lot and produced learning orders that improved student success.

sections.heading: Models worth copying
sections.md: [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint) is the survey's best curation model: small, locally specified nodes with a status each, so many humans and AI agents work in parallel and global progress is a [roll-up of node statuses](#c/c-node-status-rollup). [OpenMAIC](#c/c-openmaic) shows [human-edits-the-plan-then-agents-generate](#c/c-human-edits-plan). [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph) shows [evidence-cited edges](#c/c-evidence-cited-edges) with an independent critic. [roadmap.sh](#c/c-roadmap-sh), the [LLM Wiki](#c/c-llm-wiki) and [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything)'s [committed JSON graph](#c/c-committed-json-graph) show that [files under version control](#c/c-files-plus-git) work at scale. [Concept Catalyst](#c/c-concept-catalyst) keeps the LLM behind the UI as a suggestion generator so decisions stay with the teacher.

sections.heading: What the workflow should look like
sections.md: Every AI-made edge is a [proposal carrying confidence and cited evidence](#c/c-edge-proposals). Low-confidence or high-impact edges go to a [human review queue](#c/c-review-queue) (the ACE pattern), and the system records who approved what. In the [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack), that's a [React Flow curation UI](#c/c-curation-ui) with an accept/reject queue, backed by [concept files](#c/c-concept-files) whose git commits record provenance.

sections.heading: Who scores well on it today?
sections.md: In the comparison matrix, strong human curation comes from very different mechanisms. Oppia has creator tools; Learning Commons is expert-authored; Lean Blueprint has humans and AI working on the same graph; OpenMAIC lets people edit the outline and slides; the LLM Wiki relies on files and git; Co-STORM puts the human in the discourse; Obsidian + Breadcrumbs is fully hand-edited; roadmap.sh runs on pull requests. What's rare is strong curation *of prerequisite edges proposed by an LLM*: SyllabusGraph has the proposals but its human audit is still pending, and Understand-Anything's committed JSON is a sharing mechanism more than a review workflow.

concepts.title: Learner state
concepts.summary: What the learner has mastered, and a personalized path through the graph from there.
concepts.overview: Learner state is the rubric's test for whether a tool knows the learner: mastery tracking and a personalized path through the graph. It's not one of the four pillars, but it's what turns a concept graph into a course. [Oppia](#c/c-oppia), [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder) and [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor) score strong; [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy) is partial, since its [learning plans](#c/c-learning-plan) are personalized by target but not by tracked mastery. The survey argues that [mastery tracking](#c/c-mastery-tracking) should come from a transparent model like [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/c-bkt) or Math Academy-style [encompassing credit](#c/c-encompassing-edges), and that the learner view should show it as a [mastery overlay](#c/c-mastery-overlay).

concepts.title: Prerequisite-graph learning systems
concepts.summary: Learning systems built on prerequisite graphs: right data model, little LLM help, weak visualization.
concepts.overview: This family has what the others lack: a real [prerequisite model](#c/c-prerequisite-model). [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy) computed learning plans from a concept graph before LLMs existed, [Oppia](#c/c-oppia) runs production lessons on prerequisite skills, [Learning Commons](#c/c-learning-commons-kg) publishes vetted K-12 prerequisite data, and [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint) tracks dependencies for formal math. A set of [small DAG and mastery engines](#c/c-small-dag-engines) adds modern ideas such as evidence-cited edges and knowledge tracing. What the family lacks is LLM co-authoring and good visualization; its historical weakness was the [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck) of hand-writing every edge. The survey treats these systems as the data model and curation patterns to copy, not as platforms to adopt.

concepts.title: Small prerequisite DAG and mastery engines
concepts.summary: Tiny recent projects (0–1★) with good ideas for prerequisite graphs and mastery, not for adoption.
concepts.overview: The survey collects seven small, recent open-source projects that each try a piece of the vision. None has real adoption (0–1★), so they're worth reading for design ideas, not building on. [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph) cites evidence for every edge and adds a critic model. [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder) pairs a validated skill DAG with LangGraph agents and knowledge tracing. [OpenScienceBasedLearningPlatform](#c/c-openscience-platform) checks prerequisite cycles in CI. A propositional-logic [Math Academy clone](#c/c-propositional-logic-math-academy) flows credit to prerequisites. [Skillgraph_OS](#c/c-skillgraph-os) separates hard and soft edges, [math-concept-mapper](#c/c-math-concept-mapper) shows class-wide gaps, and [Cognitive-knowledge-graph-engine](#c/c-cognitive-kg-engine) adds mastery tracking.

concepts.title: AI tutors and course generators
concepts.summary: Hugely adopted LLM tutors and course generators with no explicit, curatable prerequisite graph.
concepts.overview: AI tutors and course generators are the most adopted learning tools in the survey. [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor) (~40k★) and [OpenMAIC](#c/c-openmaic) (~39k★) generate lessons, quizzes, interactive books, simulated classrooms and 'mastery paths'. Their LLM pillar is strong, but they have **no explicit, curatable prerequisite graph**: DeepTutor uses knowledge graphs only inside retrieval, and OpenMAIC plans with a linear outline. The survey doesn't dismiss them; it recommends [keeping the graph separate from the tutor](#c/c-separate-graph-from-tutor), with a curated DAG deciding what's next and DeepTutor- or OpenMAIC-style agents teaching it. OpenMAIC's editable outline is also a useful [curation hook](#c/c-human-edits-plan).

concepts.title: Graphs that teach (for code)
concepts.summary: Hugely adopted tools where an LLM turns a codebase into a graph and a guided tour.
concepts.overview: The 'graphs that teach' family applies the survey's exact product shape to code: an LLM builds a graph, then gives a dependency-ordered guided tour. [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything) (~84k★) and [Graphify](#c/c-graphify) (~121k★) both have huge adoption. They work well for code because dependencies can be extracted mechanically; general knowledge needs LLM-proposed and human-verified prerequisite edges instead. The survey borrows several of their choices: a separate [graph-reviewer agent](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent), a [committed JSON graph](#c/c-committed-json-graph), explained edges, and [distribution as an agent skill](#c/c-agent-skill-distribution), which it credits for their massive adoption.

concepts.title: LLM knowledge curation
concepts.summary: Human and LLM co-build a shared structure, but as a wiki or mind map, not a prerequisite DAG.
concepts.overview: LLM knowledge curation is the family where humans and LLMs build a shared body of knowledge together. Its two landmarks are Karpathy's [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/c-llm-wiki), plain markdown files an agent keeps current while a human reads and edits them, and Stanford's [Co-STORM](#c/c-co-storm), where a human joins a discussion among agents while a [dynamic mind map](#c/c-dynamic-mind-map) tracks the topic. Both score strong on human curation and LLM, which is exactly what the prerequisite systems lack. Their structure is the problem: a wiki of links or a mind-map hierarchy, not a prerequisite DAG. [NotebookLM alternatives](#c/c-notebooklm-alternatives) sit nearby as a 'learn from your sources' layer.

concepts.title: Open-source NotebookLM alternatives
concepts.summary: Open-source 'chat with your sources' tools: a learning layer, not graph tools.
concepts.overview: The survey briefly covers two open-source alternatives to Google's [NotebookLM](#c/c-notebooklm): [Open Notebook](#c/c-open-notebook) (~39.4k★, MIT) and [Khoj](#c/c-khoj) (~37.5k★, AGPL-3.0). Both support chat over your sources, and podcast generation. Open Notebook has no mind maps; Khoj can produce Mermaid mind maps. The survey files them as relevant to a 'learn from your sources' layer, grounding explanations in a learner's own material, rather than as graph tools, since neither models concepts or prerequisites.

concepts.title: Personal knowledge management with graphs
concepts.summary: The DIY route: note apps and plugins with typed links that approximate a prerequisite graph for one user.
concepts.overview: Personal knowledge management tools are the survey's DIY route. [Obsidian with the Breadcrumbs plugin](#c/c-obsidian-breadcrumbs) adds typed, directed links such as `requires`, making a real directed graph; [InfraNodus](#c/c-infranodus) finds clusters and gaps; [Logseq](#c/c-logseq) and [AFFiNE](#c/c-affine) add outlines, whiteboards and mind maps. Combined with the [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/c-llm-wiki), the survey estimates you could get about 70% of the vision in a weekend for a single user: one note per concept with a `requires:` field, an agent that proposes notes and edges reviewed through git diffs, and a Breadcrumbs or [Juggl](#c/c-juggl) view. What it lacks is a learner-facing view, mastery tracking and a shared review workflow.

concepts.title: Community roadmaps and skill maps
concepts.summary: Community-curated roadmaps and skill maps: clickable node maps ordered loosely, not by strict prerequisites.
concepts.overview: Community roadmaps are node-based maps of a field that a community curates. The giant is [roadmap.sh](#c/c-roadmap-sh) (~368k★), whose developer roadmaps keep one markdown file per node, edited through pull requests. [Learn Anything](#c/c-learn-anything) began in 2017 as community-curated mind maps and learning paths but is now effectively discontinued as open source. Smaller entries include [niyue/skillmap](#c/c-niyue-skillmap), a DSL for skill trees with prerequisite edges, and [Geekbang Skill-Map](#c/c-geekbang-skill-map). The survey draws two lessons: there's huge demand for 'show me the map, then let me click a node to learn', and node-per-file plus PR curation works at scale. Their edges are ordering, not strict prerequisites.

concepts.title: GraphRAG infrastructure
concepts.summary: Tools that extract entity/relation graphs for retrieval or agent memory: useful substrate, not pedagogy.
concepts.overview: GraphRAG and agent-memory infrastructure extracts entity and relation graphs from text for retrieval or agent memory. The survey lists [Microsoft GraphRAG](#c/c-microsoft-graphrag), [LightRAG](#c/c-lightrag), [Graphiti](#c/c-graphiti), [Cognee](#c/c-cognee), [Neo4j LLM Graph Builder](#c/c-neo4j-llm-graph-builder), [rahulnyk/knowledge_graph](#c/c-rahulnyk-knowledge-graph) and [llmgraph](#c/c-llmgraph), most with 30–40k★ and MIT or Apache licenses. None of it models 'learn A before B', and the survey says their graphs are [too noisy for teaching](#c/c-claim-graphrag-noisy): in the matrix they're strong only on LLM. Their use is as an ingestion layer that finds candidate concepts in a corpus, which the suggested stack adopts for [seed data](#c/c-seed-data).

concepts.title: Visualization building blocks
concepts.summary: Open-source graph, mind-map and canvas libraries for the curation and learner views.
concepts.overview: The survey reviews the libraries a builder would draw with. [React Flow](#c/c-react-flow) is best for an editable node-and-edge UI, the curation view. [Cytoscape.js](#c/c-cytoscape-js) brings graph algorithms and DAG layouts, and [Sigma.js](#c/c-sigma-js) renders thousands of nodes for a whole-field map. [markmap](#c/c-markmap) and [simple-mind-map](#c/c-simple-mind-map) draw tree-shaped mind maps from markdown, an easy LLM output target that can't express a DAG. [Excalidraw](#c/c-excalidraw) and [tldraw](#c/c-tldraw) are freeform canvases. The key design point is that prerequisite graphs are DAGs, not trees, and read best in a [layered layout](#c/c-layered-layout) from [dagre or ELK](#c/c-dagre-elk).

concepts.title: Closed-source reference points
concepts.summary: Commercial learning and note products the survey uses for comparison only.
concepts.overview: The survey compares against a few closed-source products. [Math Academy](#c/c-math-academy) is probably the best existing product built on a prerequisite graph, with [encompassing edges](#c/c-encompassing-edges) and diagnostic placement. [Khan Academy](#c/c-khan-academy) retired its old knowledge map and now has an LLM tutor. [NotebookLM](#c/c-notebooklm) generates mind maps from sources, but they're hierarchical and hard to edit. [Heptabase, Scrintal and Kosmik](#c/c-visual-card-whiteboards) are card whiteboards where the human builds the map, and [InfraNodus](#c/c-infranodus) is commercial text-network analysis. They set the bar for quality and show which ideas, especially Math Academy's, are worth copying into open source.

concepts.title: Research on educational knowledge graphs
concepts.summary: Papers and datasets on LLM extraction, prerequisite learning and human-in-the-loop graph building.
concepts.overview: The survey lists ten pieces of research worth knowing. On how well LLMs judge prerequisites: [K12-KGraph / K12-Bench](#c/c-k12-kgraph), [ProPRL](#c/c-proprl) and the [MDPI extraction study](#c/c-mdpi-llm-extraction). On keeping humans in the loop: [ACE](#c/c-ace) and [Concept Catalyst](#c/c-concept-catalyst). On building concept graphs: [Graphusion](#c/c-graphusion), [CourseMapper](#c/c-coursemapper) and a [systematic review](#c/c-concept-map-generation-review). On using a graph once built: mapping [tutor-chat questions to find knowledge gaps](#c/c-knowledge-gaps-tutor-chats). And for evaluation, the hand-labeled [TutorialBank and LectureBank](#c/c-tutorialbank-lecturebank) datasets. Together they justify the survey's core design choice: let LLMs propose, but have humans confirm prerequisite edges.

concepts.title: Metacademy
concepts.summary: An archived 'package manager for knowledge' that turned a target concept into an ordered learning plan.
concepts.overview: Metacademy was the original 'package manager for knowledge': concepts, mostly in machine learning and statistics, linked in a [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph). Pick a target concept and it computed a [personalized learning plan](#c/c-learning-plan): every unmet prerequisite in [topological order](#c/c-topological-order), each with curated resources and time estimates. The survey calls it the cleanest statement of the idea and its data model worth reusing. It was archived in 2023 with 688★, predates LLMs, and failed on the [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck): experts had to hand-write every node and edge. That failure is exactly what LLM-assisted curation with [human review](#c/c-human-curation) is meant to fix.

sections.heading: What did it do?
sections.md: Metacademy held concepts in a prerequisite graph, mostly machine learning and statistics. A learner picked a target concept, and it computed a personalized learning plan: all the unmet prerequisites in topological order, each with curated resources. Each concept carried its prerequisites, resources and time estimates.

sections.heading: Where does it stand now?
sections.md: It was **archived in 2023** with 688★. The code is GPL-3.0 and the content CC BY-SA, built on Python 2.7 and Django. It has no LLM features, since it predates LLMs. In the comparison matrix it scores strong on the prerequisite model and chunked nodes, partial on visualization, human curation (expert-edited) and learner state (learning plans), and none on LLM.

sections.heading: Why did it stall?
sections.md: Its downfall was the [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck): experts had to hand-write every node and edge. The survey's argument is that LLM-assisted curation fixes exactly that, provided humans still approve the prerequisite edges, since [LLMs alone are unreliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges).

sections.heading: What's worth reusing?
sections.md: The survey calls Metacademy the cleanest statement of the idea. Its data model (concept → prerequisites, plus curated resources and time estimates) is worth reusing, and its learning plan is the model for the [DAG-first visualization](#c/c-dag-first-visualization): a layered 'what do I need first?' view for one target concept.

sections.heading: What would it look like with LLMs?
sections.md: The survey's whole proposal can be read as Metacademy plus the pieces it lacked. Keep its data model and its target-based learning plan. Replace hand-writing with an agent that [proposes concepts and prerequisite edges with evidence](#c/c-edge-proposals), and a [review queue](#c/c-review-queue) where experts confirm only what matters, as [ACE](#c/c-ace) showed works. Add the visualization it only partly had, a layered view of one target's path zoomable to the whole field, and a mastery model so the plan skips what the learner knows. Keep the content in [plain files under git](#c/c-files-plus-git) so curation is shared rather than bottlenecked on a few experts.

sections.heading: Where can I read more?
sections.md: The survey links Metacademy's archived repository, its about page, an introduction on hunch.net and a retrospective on foldl.me. The retrospective is the place to look for why curation stalled, in the words of the people who ran it.

concepts.title: Oppia
concepts.summary: A nonprofit open-source lesson platform whose lessons declare prerequisite skills.
concepts.overview: Oppia is a free, nonprofit, open-source lesson platform (6.8k★, Apache-2.0, very active). Its base unit is a [skill](#c/c-skill-granularity): a concept card, worked examples and known misconceptions, phrased as 'given X, compute Y'. Lessons declare prerequisite skills, and those drive review questions at the start of each lesson. The survey values it for its battle-tested granularity, a good model for [chunked nodes](#c/c-chunked-nodes), and pairs it with [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder) as the model for learner modeling: prerequisite skills plus [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/c-bkt). Its gaps are the ones the survey is looking to fill: no learner-facing concept map and no LLM authoring of the graph.

concepts.title: Learning Commons Knowledge Graph
concepts.summary: Open, machine-readable K-12 prerequisite data from CZI with Anthropic, with an MCP server for agents.
concepts.overview: The Learning Commons Knowledge Graph, from the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative with Anthropic, is open K-12 prerequisite *data* rather than an app. It covers US standards from all 50 states in four subjects, Learning Components (granular skills that break standards down), Learning Progressions (how standards build on each other), the Math Coherence Map, standards-aligned curricula, and a curriculum dependency endpoint. It's reachable by REST API, JSONL downloads and an [MCP server](#c/c-mcp-server), which makes it directly usable by agents. The survey's advice is to [reuse it](#c/c-reuse-vetted-graphs) as a vetted prerequisite skeleton for K-12 instead of generating one, and it's the suggested [seed data](#c/c-seed-data). It is a data layer, not a viewer or editor.

concepts.title: Lean Blueprint
concepts.summary: A typed dependency graph of definitions and theorems, with per-node status, for formalizing math.
concepts.overview: Lean Blueprint describes a math formalization project as a typed dependency graph of definitions, lemmas and theorems. Dependencies are recorded explicitly, with separate lists for a statement and its proof, and each node has a status (not ready, ready, formalized) shown as colours in the rendered graph. The survey names it the best human-plus-AI curation model: because nodes are small and locally specified, many humans and AI agents can work in parallel, and global progress is just a [roll-up of node statuses](#c/c-node-status-rollup). [LeanArchitect](#c/c-leanarchitect) now infers dependencies from Lean code automatically. It applies to proofs rather than pedagogy, but its collaboration pattern and file-based workflow are what a learning graph should copy.

sections.heading: What is a blueprint?
sections.md: A blueprint is a **typed dependency graph** of definitions, lemmas and theorems for a formalization project. Dependencies are recorded explicitly, and a statement and its proof carry separate dependency lists. Each node has a status (not ready, ready, formalized), shown as colours in the rendered dependency graph.

sections.heading: Why is it the best curation model?
sections.md: Small, locally specified nodes let many humans and AI agents work in parallel, and global progress is just a [roll-up of node statuses](#c/c-node-status-rollup). The survey's TL;DR names it the model to copy for curation and data format: a typed dependency graph, per-node status, and humans and AI working side by side. It also counts it among the projects showing that [plain files plus git](#c/c-files-plus-git) beat a database for curation.

sections.heading: Where is it going?
sections.md: [LeanArchitect](#c/c-leanarchitect) (ITP 2026) extracts blueprint data from Lean code and infers dependencies automatically. [Lean Atlas](#c/c-lean-atlas) and [TheoremGraph](#c/c-theoremgraph) push it further toward human-AI collaboration. leanblueprint itself has 376★ (Apache-2.0) and is used by major formalization projects.

sections.heading: How does it score?
sections.md: Strong on the prerequisite model, chunked nodes, visual graph and human curation; partial on LLM (LeanArchitect, AI provers) and learner state (node status). The catch is the domain: it models proofs, not pedagogy. The survey suggests reusing Mathlib and blueprint dependency graphs directly for formal math rather than regenerating them.

sections.heading: How would the pattern transfer to learning?
sections.md: Swap theorems for concepts and 'formalized' for 'reviewed'. Each concept is a small file with explicit prerequisites and a status (proposed or reviewed), as in the suggested stack's concept files. Agents and people work on different concepts in parallel, and the graph's colour shows how much has been checked. The survey notes the collaboration pattern is what it wants, 'applied to proofs instead of pedagogy'. One difference matters: in Lean, a machine can verify a proof, so 'formalized' is objective. In learning, 'reviewed' is a human judgment, which is why the review queue and provenance carry more weight.

sections.heading: Where can I read more?
sections.md: The survey links the leanblueprint repository by Patrick Massot, the LeanArchitect paper, and papers on Lean Atlas and TheoremGraph.

concepts.title: LeanArchitect
concepts.summary: A 2026 tool that extracts blueprint data from Lean code and infers dependencies automatically.
concepts.overview: LeanArchitect, presented at ITP 2026, extracts [blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint) data directly from Lean code and infers the dependencies between definitions and theorems automatically. In the comparison matrix it's the reason Lean Blueprint scores partial on LLM and agent capabilities. It illustrates a point the survey makes about code tools too: where dependencies can be extracted mechanically from a formal artefact, structure can be generated reliably, whereas general knowledge needs LLM-proposed and human-verified prerequisite edges.

concepts.title: Lean Atlas
concepts.summary: A project extending Lean blueprints toward human–AI collaboration.
concepts.overview: Lean Atlas is one of two projects the survey mentions that push the [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint) approach further toward human–AI collaboration on formal mathematics, alongside [TheoremGraph](#c/c-theoremgraph). The survey gives no further detail. It matters here as evidence that the blueprint's pattern, small nodes with explicit dependencies and a status each, is becoming the shared workspace for people and AI provers in formal math, which is the collaboration model the survey wants to transfer to learning graphs.

concepts.title: TheoremGraph
concepts.summary: A project extending Lean blueprints toward human–AI collaboration.
concepts.overview: TheoremGraph, like [Lean Atlas](#c/c-lean-atlas), is cited as pushing the [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint) dependency-graph approach further toward human–AI collaboration in formal mathematics. The survey mentions it only in passing. Its relevance is as a sign of momentum: typed dependency graphs with per-node status are becoming the medium through which humans and AI agents divide up large formalization projects, the pattern the survey recommends for curating prerequisite graphs for learning.

concepts.title: SyllabusGraph
concepts.summary: An agent pipeline that turns source texts into an evidence-cited concept graph, reviewed by a critic model.
concepts.overview: SyllabusGraph is a tiny (1★) but closely watched project: a source-to-course agent pipeline that runs through Claude Code or Codex. Every concept and edge it extracts cites [evidence](#c/c-evidence-cited-edges) from the source texts, and an independent [critic model](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent) reviews the graph. It renders an interactive concept map with overview-to-detail zoom and has a notion of mastery level: 'a definition doesn't satisfy a dependency that needs a calculation', the seed of [depth-qualified prerequisites](#c/c-depth-qualified-prerequisites). Its demo turned three QFT books into 117 concepts. In the matrix it's the closest thing to all four pillars, missing only a finished human audit step, and the survey names it the model for evidence-backed LLM extraction.

sections.heading: What does it do?
sections.md: SyllabusGraph (MIT, active in September 2026) is a **source-to-course agent pipeline**. It reads source texts, extracts concepts and prerequisite edges, and builds an interactive concept map with overview-to-detail zoom. It runs through Claude Code or Codex. Its demo turned three quantum field theory books into 117 concepts.

sections.heading: What makes it different?
sections.md: Two things. Every concept and edge **cites evidence** from the source texts, and an **independent critic model** reviews the graph. The survey turns both into design rules: make every edge a [proposal with confidence and cited evidence](#c/c-edge-proposals), and give the pipeline a [critic](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent) that checks for cycles, missing prerequisites and unsupported evidence. It also has a notion of mastery level, 'a definition doesn't satisfy a dependency that needs a calculation', which the survey generalizes into [depth-qualified prerequisites](#c/c-depth-qualified-prerequisites).

sections.heading: How close is it to the full vision?
sections.md: Closer than anything else in the matrix: strong on the prerequisite model, chunked nodes, visual graph and LLM (agent plus critic), and partial on human curation (human audit pending) and learner state. Its weakness is adoption, 1★, and the survey files it among the [small DAG engines](#c/c-small-dag-engines) worth reading for ideas rather than adopting.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.md: It's the survey's pick for **evidence-backed LLM extraction**. Since [LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges), citing evidence per edge is what makes a human review fast: the reviewer checks a quote, not the whole subject.

sections.heading: What would a human audit add?
sections.md: SyllabusGraph's one partial score is human curation, with a human audit still pending. That's the piece the survey's design supplies: route low-confidence or high-impact edges to a [review queue](#c/c-review-queue), record who approved what, and mark unreviewed edges distinctly in the learner's view. Because every edge already carries evidence, SyllabusGraph is well placed for this. A reviewer can accept or reject an edge by reading its cited passage, and the critic's findings can decide which edges reach the human first.

sections.heading: What does the QFT demo show?
sections.md: Turning three quantum field theory books into 117 concepts shows the pipeline can handle dense, advanced material where prerequisites are genuinely deep. It also shows the scale at which review matters: 117 concepts imply a few hundred candidate edges, too many to check casually but few enough for a ranked queue.

concepts.title: PathFinder
concepts.summary: A hand-built, cycle-checked skill DAG with LangGraph agents and knowledge tracing that replans after quizzes.
concepts.overview: PathFinder (the Learning-Path repo, 0★) combines a hand-built skill DAG, checked for cycles with NetworkX, with [LangGraph](#c/c-langgraph) agents for gap finding, scheduling, and quiz and explanation generation. It estimates mastery with [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/c-bkt) and redoes the learning plan when quiz scores come in. The survey names it, with [Oppia](#c/c-oppia), as the model to copy for learner modeling. In the matrix it scores strong on the prerequisite model, LLM and learner state, but only partial on chunked nodes, visualization and curation, since its graph lives in JSON files edited by hand.

concepts.title: OpenScienceBasedLearningPlatform
concepts.summary: A single curriculum file with CI checks for broken references and prerequisite cycles.
concepts.overview: OpenScienceBasedLearningPlatform keeps its whole curriculum in one `curriculum.json` (tracks, modules, skills, lessons) and runs CI checks for duplicate IDs, broken references and prerequisite cycles. It has a zoomable, pannable graph view, and changes come in as pull requests. The survey borrows its main idea for the design section: when the graph lives in [plain files under git](#c/c-files-plus-git), add [CI checks for cycles and dangling references](#c/c-ci-graph-checks) so every change keeps it a valid [DAG](#c/c-dag).

concepts.title: Open-source Math Academy for propositional logic
concepts.summary: A 29-topic logic course where solving a problem gives weighted credit to its prerequisite topics.
concepts.overview: Shared on Show HN, this open-source 'Math Academy' for propositional logic is a 29-topic [prerequisite DAG](#c/c-prerequisite-graph). Its notable idea is that solving a problem gives fractional credit to the prerequisite topics, weighted by edge weight: a Math Academy-style implicit repetition, where practising something advanced counts as review of what it builds on. The survey generalizes this as [encompassing edges](#c/c-encompassing-edges), one of its proposed edge types, and as a transparent alternative to LLM judgment for [mastery tracking](#c/c-mastery-tracking).

concepts.title: Skillgraph_OS
concepts.summary: A skill DAG with separate 'prerequisite' and 'helps-with' edges and alternative routes.
concepts.overview: Skillgraph_OS is a small skill DAG with two edge types, 'prerequisite' and 'helps-with', plus alternative routes through the graph. It's an early example of the survey's recommendation to [distinguish edge types](#c/c-edge-types): a [hard prerequisite](#c/c-hard-prerequisite) you can't skip versus a [soft one](#c/c-soft-prerequisite) that only makes learning easier. Alternative routes matter because a DAG usually admits several valid reading orders, and learners arrive with different backgrounds.

concepts.title: math-concept-mapper
concepts.summary: A teacher-facing concept-map editor with a class dashboard of prerequisite gaps and AI suggestions.
concepts.overview: math-concept-mapper is a concept-map editor built for teachers rather than learners. Its class dashboard highlights hub and isolated concepts and class-wide prerequisite gaps, and it offers AI recommendations. It's one of the [small DAG engines](#c/c-small-dag-engines) the survey reads for ideas: using the prerequisite graph to diagnose a whole class, not just one learner, echoing research that maps tutor-chat questions onto a prerequisite graph to find [knowledge gaps](#c/c-knowledge-gaps-tutor-chats).

concepts.title: Cognitive-knowledge-graph-engine
concepts.summary: A prerequisite-aware graph with mastery tracking and recommendations.
concepts.overview: Cognitive-knowledge-graph-engine is a small project combining a prerequisite-aware graph with [mastery tracking](#c/c-mastery-tracking) and recommendations of what to study next. The survey lists it without further comment among the [small DAG engines](#c/c-small-dag-engines): a pattern to read, not a platform to adopt. Together with [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder), it shows that joining a [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph) with a learner model is a common first step for builders in this space.

concepts.title: DeepTutor
concepts.summary: The strongest open-source LLM tutor: RAG, tutoring, quizzes and mastery paths, but no prerequisite graph.
concepts.overview: DeepTutor, from the HKU Data Science Lab (~40.3k★, Apache-2.0, releases every few days), is an 'agent-native' learning workspace: [RAG](#c/c-rag) over your materials, tutoring chat, problem solving, quiz generation, interactive books, persistent AI partners, mastery paths with progression gates, a three-layer learner memory, Mermaid and HTML visualizations and a skills marketplace. The survey calls it the strongest open-source LLM tutor foundation. Its gap is the graph: knowledge graphs are used only inside retrieval, and there's no curated, learner-visible [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph). The suggested pairing is a curated concept DAG that decides *what's next* and DeepTutor-style agents that *teach it*.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.md: An **agent-native learning workspace** from the HKU Data Science Lab, with ~40.3k★ under Apache-2.0 and releases every few days. It went from zero to 20k★ in 111 days. It's built on Python/FastAPI and Next.js.

sections.heading: What does it do?
sections.md: It offers [RAG](#c/c-rag) over your materials (through LlamaIndex, [GraphRAG](#c/c-microsoft-graphrag), [LightRAG](#c/c-lightrag) and others); tutoring chat, problem solving, quiz generation and 'interactive books'; persistent AI 'partners'; **mastery paths with progression gates**; a three-layer learner memory; Mermaid and HTML visualizations; and a skills marketplace.

sections.heading: What's missing?
sections.md: The graph. DeepTutor uses knowledge graphs *inside retrieval*. There's no curated, learner-visible prerequisite graph and no documented prerequisite modeling, so its 'mastery paths' can't be inspected or corrected by a curator. In the matrix it scores none on the prerequisite model, partial on chunked nodes, visual graph (Mermaid) and curation, and strong on LLM and learner state.

sections.heading: How would it fit?
sections.md: The survey's takeaway is to **pair it with a curated concept DAG**: the graph decides *what's next*, and DeepTutor-style agents *teach it*. That's the design rule [keep the graph separate from the tutor](#c/c-separate-graph-from-tutor), with the tutor generating explanations and quizzes for one node at a time and mastery coming from a transparent model rather than the LLM.

sections.heading: What are 'mastery paths' without a graph?
sections.md: DeepTutor's mastery paths gate progression on the learner's performance, but the order of topics comes from the model rather than an explicit, inspectable graph. That works for one learner's session, but a teacher or curator can't see why one topic comes before another, fix a wrong ordering once for everyone, or reuse the structure elsewhere. The survey's point isn't that DeepTutor teaches badly; it's that the *what next* decision should come from a curated graph that people can review.

sections.heading: Why is it the foundation to pair with, not replace?
sections.md: Its adoption and pace (~40k★, releases every few days) mean it's where much of the open-source LLM-tutoring effort is going. It already does the *how*: tutoring, quizzes, learner memory and visualizations. Building a competing tutor would duplicate that. Building a curated graph that a DeepTutor-style tutor can consume adds the missing piece.

concepts.title: OpenMAIC
concepts.summary: Turns a topic into a multi-agent classroom, with a human-editable outline before generation.
concepts.overview: OpenMAIC, from Tsinghua (~38.9k★, MIT, v1.0 in August 2026), turns a topic or document into a multi-agent classroom: an AI teacher, a TA and classmates, with slides, quizzes, simulations and project-based learning. Its pipeline goes from outline to scenes, and the outline is human-editable before anything is generated, with 'Edit with AI' applying validated JSON-patch edits. The survey's takeaway is that pattern, [human edits the plan, then agents generate](#c/c-human-edits-plan), where the outline is the curation hook. Its gap is structure: a linear course outline, not a graph, with no prerequisite modeling.

concepts.title: Understand-Anything
concepts.summary: A multi-agent pipeline that turns a codebase into a knowledge graph with dependency-ordered guided tours.
concepts.overview: Understand-Anything (~84k★, MIT) runs a multi-agent pipeline, a scanner, file and architecture analyzers, a tour-builder and a graph-reviewer, that turns a codebase into an interactive, force-directed knowledge graph. It supports semantic search and Q&A over the graph, and its [guided tours](#c/c-guided-tour) walk through the architecture in dependency order. The graph is [committed as JSON](#c/c-committed-json-graph), so teams share it and a read-only viewer needs no LLM. Its tagline is 'Graphs that teach > graphs that impress'. The survey says this *is* the product shape it's after, in the wrong domain: code dependencies can be extracted mechanically, while general knowledge needs LLM-proposed, human-verified prerequisites.

sections.heading: What does it do?
sections.md: A multi-agent pipeline (a scanner, file and architecture analyzers, a **tour-builder** and a **graph-reviewer**) turns a codebase into an interactive force-directed knowledge graph. It adds semantic search and Q&A over the graph, and **guided tours that walk through the architecture ordered by dependency**. Its tagline: 'Graphs that teach > graphs that impress.'

sections.heading: Why does the survey call it 'your product shape'?
sections.md: Because it's the UX the survey is looking for, 'LLM builds a graph, then gives a guided tour', and it has massive adoption (~84k★). The TL;DR names it the UX reference. The difference is the domain. Code dependencies can be extracted mechanically, so the graph can be trusted; general knowledge needs LLM-proposed and human-verified prerequisite edges instead.

sections.heading: What's worth copying?
sections.md: Two things, says the survey: the separate **graph-reviewer agent**, which becomes the [critic](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent) in the suggested stack, and the **[committed JSON graph](#c/c-committed-json-graph)**, which lets teams share the graph through git and view it with no LLM. It's also one of the two projects, with [Graphify](#c/c-graphify), that reached massive adoption by [shipping as a skill](#c/c-agent-skill-distribution) for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.

sections.heading: How does it score?
sections.md: Strong on the prerequisite model (code dependencies), chunked nodes, visual graph and LLM (multi-agent plus reviewer); partial on human curation (a committed JSON file, not a review workflow); none on learner state. Its [force-directed layout](#c/c-force-directed-layout) is the one thing the survey would change for learners, preferring a [layered layout](#c/c-layered-layout).

sections.heading: What would it take to adapt it to general knowledge?
sections.md: The pipeline's shape carries over: scan sources, build a graph, review it with a separate agent, commit it as a file, and generate a tour. What changes is the edge source. In code, a dependency is a fact in the syntax tree; in a textbook, 'you need A before B' is a judgment that LLMs get right only about half the time. So the scanner becomes a [proposer](#c/c-proposer-agent) that cites evidence, the graph-reviewer becomes a [critic](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent), and a [human review queue](#c/c-review-queue) sits between them and the committed graph. The guided tour becomes a [learning plan](#c/c-learning-plan) over reviewed prerequisites.

concepts.title: Graphify
concepts.summary: An agent skill that turns any folder into a local, queryable knowledge graph with every edge explained.
concepts.overview: Graphify (~121k★, Apache-2.0) ships as a `/graphify` skill for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other agents. It turns any folder, code, docs, PDFs, images or video, into a local, queryable knowledge graph, using deterministic AST parsing where it can, explaining every edge, and needing no Neo4j or vector store. The survey reads it as validating a distribution model, [agent skill plus local graph file plus explained edges](#c/c-agent-skill-distribution), and cites its adoption as evidence that [shipping as a skill drives adoption](#c/c-claim-skills-drive-adoption). Its limit for learning: its edges are relations, not pedagogy. It's also suggested as an ingestion pass for [seed data](#c/c-seed-data).

concepts.title: LLM Wiki pattern
concepts.summary: Karpathy's pattern: raw sources plus an LLM-maintained markdown wiki that a human reads and edits.
concepts.overview: The LLM Wiki is a pattern, not a product, from a viral April 2026 post by [Andrej Karpathy](#c/c-andrej-karpathy). A `raw/` folder holds immutable sources, a `wiki/` folder holds LLM-written, interlinked markdown pages, and a schema file (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md) governs the agent. The human reads and edits in Obsidian while the agent keeps the wiki current. It spread fast, with an Obsidian plugin, the llm-wiki-kit MCP server and a Hermes Agent skill. The survey calls it the most popular human-plus-LLM curation workflow today: plain files, git, and an agent governed by a schema. Its gap is structure, links only; adding typed `prerequisites:` frontmatter would get most of the way to a curatable concept DAG.

sections.heading: How does the pattern work?
sections.md: Three parts. `raw/` holds **immutable sources**. `wiki/` holds **LLM-written, interlinked markdown pages**. A **schema file** (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md) tells the agent how to maintain the wiki. The human reads and edits in Obsidian, and the agent keeps the wiki current as sources arrive.

sections.heading: Where did it come from?
sections.md: [Andrej Karpathy](#c/c-andrej-karpathy) described it in April 2026 in a viral post on X, with a gist that gained 5k+★ in days. It isn't a product, but it has implementations: an Obsidian plugin, `llm-wiki-kit` (an MCP server) and a Hermes Agent skill. [InfraNodus](#c/c-infranodus) also ships an LLM-Wiki mode.

sections.heading: Why does it matter here?
sections.md: The survey calls it the most popular human-plus-LLM curation workflow right now: plain files, git, and a schema-governed agent. It's one of the projects behind the claim that [plain files plus git beat a database](#c/c-claim-files-git-beats-db), and the TL;DR lists it with Co-STORM as the leading examples of LLM knowledge curation. In the matrix it's strong on chunked nodes, LLM and human curation (files plus git), partial on visuals (through Obsidian), and none on prerequisites and learner state.

sections.heading: How close is it to a learning graph?
sections.md: One step away, says the survey: **add typed `prerequisites:` frontmatter** and you're most of the way to a curatable concept DAG. The DIY route spells this out: one note per concept with a `requires:` field, an agent that proposes notes and edges reviewed through git diffs, and a [Breadcrumbs](#c/c-obsidian-breadcrumbs) or [Juggl](#c/c-juggl) view, about 70% of the vision in a weekend for one user.

sections.heading: What's missing for learners?
sections.md: The DIY route built on it lacks three things, says the survey: a learner-facing view, mastery tracking, and a shared review workflow. The LLM Wiki is designed for one person curating their own knowledge in Obsidian. A learning product needs a view built for someone who doesn't yet know the subject, a model of what they've mastered, and a way for several curators to review what the agent proposes. Those are exactly the parts the [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack) adds around a wiki-like folder of [concept files](#c/c-concept-files).

concepts.title: Co-STORM
concepts.summary: Stanford's system where a human joins AI experts while a dynamic mind map tracks the topic.
concepts.overview: STORM, from Stanford OVAL (~31.5k★, MIT), researches a topic and writes a cited, Wikipedia-style article. Its extension Co-STORM lets a human join a discussion among AI 'experts' and a moderator, while the system keeps a [dynamic mind map](#c/c-dynamic-mind-map): a hierarchical concept structure that serves as a shared conceptual space between human and system. The survey calls it the best-studied design for human-plus-LLM co-exploration of a topic, strong on LLM and human curation. But its structure is a taxonomy, not prerequisites, so it can't say what to learn first, and activity has slowed, with the last push in September 2025.

concepts.title: Open Notebook
concepts.summary: An open-source NotebookLM alternative for chat, sources and podcasts, with no mind maps.
concepts.overview: Open Notebook (~39.4k★, MIT) is an open-source alternative to [NotebookLM](#c/c-notebooklm): you add sources, chat with them and generate podcasts. The survey notes explicitly that it has no mind maps, unlike [Khoj](#c/c-khoj) or NotebookLM itself. Its popularity shows strong demand for learning from one's own sources, but it has no concept or prerequisite structure. The survey treats it as a possible 'learn from your sources' layer next to a learning graph, not as a graph tool.

concepts.title: Khoj
concepts.summary: An open-source NotebookLM alternative that can generate Mermaid mind maps.
concepts.overview: Khoj (~37.5k★, AGPL-3.0) is another open-source alternative to [NotebookLM](#c/c-notebooklm) for chatting with your sources. Unlike [Open Notebook](#c/c-open-notebook), it can produce Mermaid mind maps. Those maps are hierarchies, like NotebookLM's and Co-STORM's, so they show how a topic breaks down but not what to learn first. The survey counts Khoj as part of a 'learn from your sources' layer rather than a graph tool, and its AGPL license is worth noting for anyone building on it.

concepts.title: Obsidian + Breadcrumbs
concepts.summary: Obsidian notes plus the Breadcrumbs plugin's typed, directed links, forming a real directed graph.
concepts.overview: Obsidian is a closed-source (free) note app; Breadcrumbs (~800★) is an open-source plugin that adds typed, directed links, up, down, next, previous or custom ones such as `requires`, defined in frontmatter, and builds a real directed graph from them. That makes it the quickest way to a working [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph) prototype today, especially combined with the [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/c-llm-wiki). In the matrix it's strong on everything except LLM (only through plugins) and learner state. Its limits are the DIY route's: one user, no learner-facing view, no mastery tracking, no shared review workflow.

concepts.title: InfraNodus
concepts.summary: Text-network analysis that shows topical clusters, central ideas and gaps between clusters.
concepts.overview: InfraNodus is a commercial text-network analysis service with an AGPL-3.0 Obsidian plugin (172★), the AI Graph View. It finds topical clusters, central ideas and, most interestingly for learning, gaps between clusters. It also ships an [LLM-Wiki](#c/c-llm-wiki) mode. The survey lists it under the [DIY PKM route](#c/c-pkm-graphs) and again among closed-source reference points, since the backend is a commercial SaaS. Its gap-finding is a different notion from a missing prerequisite: it finds topics that aren't connected, not foundations a learner lacks.

concepts.title: Logseq
concepts.summary: An open-source outliner with a graph view and whiteboards.
concepts.overview: Logseq (~45k★, AGPL-3.0) is an open-source outliner with a graph view and whiteboards. The survey lists it among the [personal knowledge management tools](#c/c-pkm-graphs) that could host a do-it-yourself concept graph. Its links are untyped by default, so like most PKM graph views it shows what's connected rather than what must come first. It's an alternative base to Obsidian for someone assembling the DIY route, with the advantage of being open source throughout.

concepts.title: AFFiNE
concepts.summary: A local-first, open-source mix of docs, whiteboard and mind map, with AI features.
concepts.overview: AFFiNE (~73k★) combines documents, a whiteboard and a mind map in a local-first, open-source app with AI features. The survey lists it under the [DIY PKM route](#c/c-pkm-graphs) and flags its mixed license: check it before building on it. Like other mind-map tools, it structures knowledge as a hierarchy rather than a [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph), so it would need typed links added before it could answer 'what do I need first?'.

concepts.title: Juggl
concepts.summary: An Obsidian graph-view plugin suggested for viewing a DIY concept graph.
concepts.overview: Juggl is an Obsidian plugin for interactive graph views. The survey names it, alongside [Breadcrumbs](#c/c-obsidian-breadcrumbs), as the viewer for the DIY route: one note per concept with a `requires:` field, an agent proposing notes and edges reviewed through git diffs, and a Breadcrumbs or Juggl view to see the result. It's mentioned only in that recipe, as the visual layer of a single-user prototype built on the [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/c-llm-wiki), not as a learner-facing view.

concepts.title: roadmap.sh
concepts.summary: Hugely popular developer roadmaps with one markdown file per node, under a restrictive license.
concepts.overview: roadmap.sh (the developer-roadmap repo, ~368k★) is one of GitHub's most-starred repositories: interactive, node-based roadmaps for developer roles, where each node's content is a markdown file edited through community pull requests. The hosted site adds an AI roadmap generator and AI tutor, but those aren't in the open repo. The survey takes two lessons from it: it proves the demand for 'show me the map, then let me click a node to learn', and it proves that [node-per-file plus PR curation](#c/c-files-plus-git) works at scale. Two cautions: its edges are roadmap order, not strict prerequisites, and its custom license allows personal use only, so you can study it but not build on it.

concepts.title: Learn Anything
concepts.summary: Community-curated mind maps and learning paths from 2017, now effectively discontinued as open source.
concepts.overview: Learn Anything began in 2017 as open-source, community-curated mind maps and learning paths, and later described itself as 'AI- and community-guided'. The original repository (16.9k★) now holds a different, dormant project called Linsa, so it's effectively discontinued as open source, and the survey treats it as a historical reference. It's still cited, with [roadmap.sh](#c/c-roadmap-sh), as proof that keeping curated knowledge in [files under version control](#c/c-files-plus-git) works, and as an early attempt at the survey's vision that didn't survive.

concepts.title: skillmap (niyue)
concepts.summary: A text DSL that renders a skill tree with progress bars and prerequisite edges.
concepts.overview: skillmap, by niyue, is a small text DSL: you describe skills and their prerequisites in plain text and it renders a skill tree with progress bars and prerequisite edges. The survey lists it under 'Others' among the [community roadmaps and skill maps](#c/c-community-roadmaps). It's a reminder that a text format can be an easy target for both people and LLMs to write, and that progress shown on the map, a simple [mastery overlay](#c/c-mastery-overlay), makes a skill tree motivating.

concepts.title: Geekbang Skill-Map
concepts.summary: Programmer skill maps, mirrored on SourceForge.
concepts.overview: Geekbang Skill-Map is a set of programmer skill maps, listed by the survey under 'Others' with a SourceForge mirror as its link. The survey gives no further detail. It belongs with [roadmap.sh](#c/c-roadmap-sh) and [niyue/skillmap](#c/c-niyue-skillmap) as evidence that developers in particular want maps of what to learn, and like them its structure is an ordering of skills rather than a validated [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph).

concepts.title: GraphRAG (Microsoft)
concepts.summary: Microsoft's library that builds community summaries over an LLM-extracted entity graph.
concepts.overview: microsoft/graphrag (36k★, MIT) is the project that gave [GraphRAG](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure) its name as a category. It extracts an entity graph from a corpus with an LLM, groups it into communities and writes community summaries that improve retrieval for broad questions. [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor) is among the tools that use GraphRAG for retrieval over a learner's materials. For the survey's purposes it's substrate: its relations describe entities in the text, not the order in which concepts should be learned.

concepts.title: LightRAG
concepts.summary: A lighter GraphRAG with a built-in graph viewer, used by DeepTutor.
concepts.overview: LightRAG, from HKUDS (39.8k★, MIT), is a lighter-weight take on [GraphRAG](#c/c-microsoft-graphrag) that also ships a graph viewer. It's used by [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor), from the same lab, for retrieval over a learner's materials. The survey's suggested stack names it as a model for ingestion: a LightRAG- or Graphify-style pass over a user's corpus can produce the candidate concepts that become [seed data](#c/c-seed-data), before the proposer agent and human review turn them into a prerequisite graph.

concepts.title: Graphiti
concepts.summary: A temporal knowledge graph for agent memory, from Zep.
concepts.overview: Graphiti, from getzep (31.1k★, Apache-2.0), is a temporal knowledge graph for agent memory: it records facts along with when they held, so an agent can remember and reason over a changing world. The survey lists it under [GraphRAG and agent-memory infrastructure](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure), useful substrate but not pedagogy. Its temporal angle doesn't map onto learning directly, though a learner's changing mastery is a kind of time-varying state an agent might want to remember.

concepts.title: Cognee
concepts.summary: Memory and knowledge-graph pipelines for AI agents.
concepts.overview: Cognee, from topoteretes (31k★, Apache-2.0), provides memory and knowledge-graph pipelines for AI applications. The survey lists it among the [GraphRAG and agent-memory tools](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure) that extract entity and relation graphs from text. Like the others, it doesn't model prerequisites, so its graphs aren't a learning structure on their own. At most, it could serve as the pipeline that turns a corpus into candidate concepts for a human-reviewed [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph).

concepts.title: Neo4j LLM Graph Builder
concepts.summary: Turns PDFs, YouTube videos and web pages into a Neo4j knowledge graph, with a UI.
concepts.overview: Neo4j LLM Graph Builder, from Neo4j Labs (5.3k★, Apache-2.0), uses an LLM to turn PDFs, YouTube videos and web pages into a knowledge graph stored in Neo4j, and gives you a UI to do it. It's one of the [GraphRAG infrastructure](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure) tools the survey lists. It shows how easy it has become to get *a* graph out of documents, which sharpens the survey's point: the hard part is not extraction but getting correct prerequisite edges, where [LLMs alone are unreliable](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges).

concepts.title: rahulnyk/knowledge_graph
concepts.summary: A simple tool that turns text into a concept graph.
concepts.overview: rahulnyk/knowledge_graph (4.1k★, MIT) is a simple text-to-concept-graph tool, listed among the [GraphRAG infrastructure](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure) projects. Unlike the entity-focused tools, it extracts concepts, which puts it a little closer to a learning graph. But its edges are associations found in the text, not 'learn A before B', so it would at most supply candidate concepts. It shouldn't be confused with a [knowledge graph](#c/c-knowledge-graph) in general, or with the Learning Commons Knowledge Graph.

concepts.title: llmgraph
concepts.summary: Recursively expands a topic into a knowledge graph from an LLM's own knowledge.
concepts.overview: llmgraph, by dylanhogg (509★, MIT), recursively expands a topic into a knowledge graph using the LLM's own knowledge rather than source documents. The survey calls it the closest of the GraphRAG-family tools to 'generate a concept map for X'. That's also its weakness for learning: with no sources, nothing grounds its edges, whereas the survey wants every edge to carry [cited evidence](#c/c-evidence-cited-edges) and pass [human review](#c/c-review-queue), since [LLMs alone are unreliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges).

concepts.title: React Flow
concepts.summary: A React library for editable node-and-edge UIs, best suited to the curation view.
concepts.overview: React Flow, the xyflow project (38.5k★), is a React library for node-and-edge interfaces that users can edit: drag nodes, draw edges, select and delete. The survey rates it best for an editable UI, which makes it the natural base for curation, and recommends pairing it with [ELK or dagre](#c/c-dagre-elk) to get a [layered DAG layout](#c/c-layered-layout). In the [suggested starting stack](#c/c-starting-stack), the [curation UI](#c/c-curation-ui) is a React Flow editor with an accept/reject queue for proposed edges.

concepts.title: Cytoscape.js
concepts.summary: A graph library with algorithms and many layouts, including dagre and klay for DAGs.
concepts.overview: Cytoscape.js (11.2k★) is a graph visualization and analysis library with built-in graph algorithms and many layouts, including dagre and klay, which suit prerequisite [DAGs](#c/c-dag). The survey suggests it, or [Sigma.js](#c/c-sigma-js), for the [learner UI](#c/c-learner-ui): a [layered layout](#c/c-layered-layout), a [mastery overlay](#c/c-mastery-overlay), and a 'plan my path to X' action. Its algorithms matter for learning graphs, since computing a learner's path is a graph traversal.

concepts.title: Sigma.js
concepts.summary: A WebGL graph renderer that handles thousands of nodes, for a whole-field map.
concepts.overview: Sigma.js (12.2k★) renders graphs with WebGL and handles thousands of nodes, which is what a whole-field 'map of knowledge' needs. The survey's [DAG-first visualization](#c/c-dag-first-visualization) zooms from one target's layered prerequisites out to a whole-field map at Sigma.js scale, and the suggested [learner UI](#c/c-learner-ui) uses Sigma.js or [Cytoscape.js](#c/c-cytoscape-js). It trades Cytoscape's algorithm library for raw rendering scale.

concepts.title: markmap
concepts.summary: Renders tree-shaped mind maps from markdown; easy for LLMs, but can't express a DAG.
concepts.overview: markmap (13.1k★) turns a markdown outline into an interactive, tree-shaped mind map. The survey notes why it's tempting: markdown is an easy output target for an LLM, so a mind map is one prompt away. But a tree can't express a [DAG](#c/c-dag): a concept with two prerequisites has two parents, which a mind map can't show. The survey pairs it with [simple-mind-map](#c/c-simple-mind-map) under the same verdict, and it's the reason 'DAGs, not trees' is one of its layout rules.

concepts.title: simple-mind-map
concepts.summary: A mind-map library for tree-shaped maps; like markmap, it can't express a DAG.
concepts.overview: simple-mind-map (12.8k★) is a mind-map library that the survey groups with [markmap](#c/c-markmap). Both draw tree-shaped maps and both are easy targets for LLM output, but neither can express a [DAG](#c/c-dag), since a tree gives every concept a single parent while a prerequisite graph often gives it several. For a learning graph they could at most show a topic hierarchy, like an outline, next to the real prerequisite view.

concepts.title: Excalidraw
concepts.summary: A popular freeform drawing canvas.
concepts.overview: Excalidraw (133k★) is a freeform, hand-drawn-style canvas and one of the most popular projects in the survey's visualization list. The survey lists it with [tldraw](#c/c-tldraw) as a freeform canvas: good for sketching and whiteboarding, but it has no notion of nodes, typed edges or layout, so any concept-graph structure would have to be built on top. It's the open-source counterpart to the card whiteboards like Heptabase, where the human builds the map by hand.

concepts.title: tldraw
concepts.summary: A freeform canvas library that needs a commercial license for production.
concepts.overview: tldraw (51k★) is a freeform canvas library, listed with [Excalidraw](#c/c-excalidraw). The survey's one caution is its license: tldraw needs a commercial license for production use, which matters for anyone building a product on it. Like Excalidraw, it provides a canvas rather than a graph model, so a prerequisite structure and [layered layout](#c/c-layered-layout) would need to come from elsewhere.

concepts.title: dagre / ELK
concepts.summary: Layout engines that arrange a DAG in layers, used with React Flow or Cytoscape.js.
concepts.overview: dagre and ELK are graph layout engines that compute [layered (Sugiyama) layouts](#c/c-layered-layout) for directed graphs: they assign each node a layer so that edges flow one way, then order nodes within layers to reduce crossings. The survey recommends pairing [React Flow](#c/c-react-flow) with ELK or dagre for the editable curation view, and notes that [Cytoscape.js](#c/c-cytoscape-js) includes dagre and klay layouts. The suggested learner UI uses a dagre or ELK layered layout, which is what makes 'what do I need first?' readable.

concepts.title: Math Academy
concepts.summary: Probably the best product built on a hand-curated prerequisite graph, with implicit review credit.
concepts.overview: Math Academy is a closed-source product that the survey calls probably the best existing product built on a prerequisite knowledge graph. Its topic graph is hand-curated and includes 'encompassing' edges: practising an advanced topic gives implicit review credit to the prerequisites it encompasses, so review happens without separate drills. It also uses diagnostic placement to find where a learner starts. The survey borrows the idea twice, as an [edge type](#c/c-encompassing-edges) and as a transparent way to do [mastery tracking](#c/c-mastery-tracking), and an open-source [propositional-logic clone](#c/c-propositional-logic-math-academy) already applies it.

concepts.title: Khan Academy
concepts.summary: Retired its exercise 'knowledge map'; Khanmigo is now its LLM tutor.
concepts.overview: Khan Academy once had a 'knowledge map', a graph of its exercises that learners could explore, but retired it. Its current AI offering is Khanmigo, an LLM tutor. The survey lists it only as a closed-source reference point. It's a telling one: a major learning platform moved from a visible graph to an LLM tutor, the same split the survey sees in open source between [prerequisite-graph systems](#c/c-prerequisite-graph-learning-systems) and [AI tutors](#c/c-ai-tutors), and which it proposes to reunite by [keeping the graph separate from the tutor](#c/c-separate-graph-from-tutor).

concepts.title: NotebookLM
concepts.summary: Google's source-grounded assistant, which auto-generates hierarchical, hard-to-edit mind maps.
concepts.overview: NotebookLM auto-generates mind maps from the sources you give it. The survey treats it as a closed-source reference point and notes the limits: the maps are hierarchical, not prerequisite-based, and hard to edit. That's the pattern the survey wants to move past. A mind map shows how a topic breaks down but not what to learn first, and a map a person can't edit can't be curated. Its open-source alternatives, [Open Notebook](#c/c-open-notebook) and [Khoj](#c/c-khoj), share the same 'learn from your sources' focus.

concepts.title: Heptabase / Scrintal / Kosmik
concepts.summary: Visual card whiteboards for studying, where the human builds the map by hand.
