concepts.overview: Heptabase, Scrintal and Kosmik are closed-source visual whiteboards where you study by arranging cards and drawing connections. The survey lists them as reference points and notes the key difference from its vision: the human builds the map. There's no model proposing concepts or prerequisites, which avoids LLM errors but brings back the [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck) that sank Metacademy, scaled down to one student.

concepts.title: LangGraph
concepts.summary: An agent orchestration framework used by PathFinder and OpenMAIC.
concepts.overview: LangGraph is an agent framework that both [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder) and [OpenMAIC](#c/c-openmaic) are built on. In PathFinder it runs the agents for gap finding, scheduling, and quiz and explanation generation over a hand-built skill DAG; OpenMAIC uses it with Next.js for its multi-agent classroom. The survey mentions it only as part of these stacks, but it shows the usual split: a framework orchestrates several specialized agents around a shared structure, which is how the [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack) divides the work between proposer, critic and tutor.

concepts.title: K12-KGraph / K12-Bench
concepts.summary: A 2026 curriculum KG and benchmark where frontier LLMs score only 46–57% on prerequisite reasoning.
concepts.overview: K12-KGraph (2026) is a curriculum-aligned knowledge graph built with an LLM extraction pipeline, and K12-Bench is its benchmark. On prerequisite reasoning, Gemini-3-Flash scores 57% exact match and Gemma-4-31B 46%. The authors' conclusion, which the survey adopts as a headline, is that [LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges). That single result drives much of the survey's design: every AI-made edge should be a [proposal with confidence and evidence](#c/c-edge-proposals), uncertain edges should go to a [human review queue](#c/c-review-queue), and mastery shouldn't be left to LLM judgment either.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.md: K12-KGraph is a **curriculum-aligned knowledge graph** for K-12 education built with an LLM extraction pipeline, published in 2026. K12-Bench is the benchmark that comes with it, including a prerequisite-reasoning task: given two concepts, does one require the other?

sections.heading: What did it find?
sections.md: On prerequisite reasoning, **Gemini-3-Flash scores 57% and Gemma-4-31B 46% exact match**. The TL;DR summarizes this as frontier LLMs scoring only ~46–57%. The paper's own conclusion: **LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges.**

sections.heading: Why does it matter so much here?
sections.md: Because prerequisite edges are the survey's core data, and [errors there cost learners the most](#c/c-claim-prereq-errors-costly): a missing or backwards prerequisite sends a learner into material they can't yet follow. If the best models are right only about half the time, an LLM-built prerequisite graph can't ship unreviewed. The survey's TL;DR opens its research point with this result: 'Research shows why human curation is needed.'

sections.heading: What follows from it?
sections.md: Three design rules. Every AI-made edge is a [proposal carrying confidence and cited evidence](#c/c-edge-proposals). Low-confidence or high-impact edges go to a [human review queue](#c/c-review-queue), with [ACE](#c/c-ace) as the blueprint. And [mastery comes from a transparent model](#c/c-claim-transparent-mastery), not LLM judgment. The [MDPI study](#c/c-mdpi-llm-extraction)'s finding that few-shot examples help prerequisites most suggests how to raise the model's hit rate before review.

sections.heading: How should the numbers be read?
sections.md: Exact match is a strict measure: a model has to get the relation exactly right, direction included. Some misses may be near misses, a soft prerequisite called hard or the reverse. But for a learner, direction and hardness are exactly what matter, so strictness is appropriate. The results are also for K-12 material, where concepts are well defined; the survey gives no reason to expect better on messier, advanced subjects. The two models tested are a fast frontier model and a mid-size open model, so the range 46–57% brackets what builders are likely to use in a pipeline.

sections.heading: Where can I read more?
sections.md: The paper is on arXiv; the survey cites it in both the TL;DR and the research table.

concepts.title: ACE
concepts.summary: AI-assisted construction of educational KGs: experts confirm only the top-ranked candidate edges.
concepts.overview: ACE, AI-Assisted Construction of Educational Knowledge Graphs (JEDM, 2024), scores candidate concept pairs, sends only the top-ranked ones to experts, and infers further edges from what the experts confirm. It cut expert effort a lot, and students who studied in ACE's order had better success rates. Its dataset and code are on GitHub. The survey calls it the **blueprint for the review queue**: it's the evidence that [ranking candidate edges for expert review cuts effort and improves learning orders](#c/c-claim-human-review-cuts-effort), and the pattern behind routing low-confidence or high-impact edges to a [human review queue](#c/c-review-queue).

sections.heading: How does ACE work?
sections.md: It **scores concept pairs** as candidate prerequisite edges, **sends the top-ranked candidates to experts**, and **infers more edges** from what the experts confirm. Experts only look at the edges most likely to matter, and each confirmation pays off more than once.

sections.heading: What did it achieve?
sections.md: A big cut in expert effort, and a learning outcome: students who studied in ACE's order had better success rates. The TL;DR summarizes it as cutting expert effort a lot while producing learning orders that improved student success. The dataset and code are on GitHub. It was published in the Journal of Educational Data Mining in 2024.

sections.heading: Why is it the review-queue blueprint?
sections.md: It solves both halves of the curation problem at once. Hand curation alone hits the [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck) that sank Metacademy; LLMs alone are [unreliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges). ACE ranks machine suggestions and spends human attention only where it counts. The survey's first design implication builds on it: route low-confidence or high-impact edges to a [human review queue](#c/c-review-queue) and record who approved what.

sections.heading: How would it fit a modern tool?
sections.md: In the [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack), a [proposer agent](#c/c-proposer-agent) produces edges with confidence and citations, a [critic](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent) checks them, and the [curation UI](#c/c-curation-ui) shows an accept/reject queue. ACE's contribution is the ordering of that queue: rank by expected value, so a curator's first few decisions resolve the most uncertainty.

sections.heading: What's the general lesson?
sections.md: Human attention is the scarce resource, so spend it where the model is least sure and the stakes are highest. Ranking lets a curator stop after the most valuable decisions instead of working through everything, and inferring edges from confirmed ones multiplies each decision's effect. Measuring learning outcomes, not just edge accuracy, is also worth copying: the point of a correct prerequisite graph is that students do better following it, and ACE showed they did.

concepts.title: Concept Catalyst
concepts.summary: A 2026 study where teachers build concept maps and the LLM only suggests, from behind the UI.
concepts.overview: Concept Catalyst (2026) studies teachers building concept maps with an LLM that stays behind the interface as a suggestion generator. The teacher makes every decision; the model only offers options. The survey lists it as research worth knowing because it's another answer to the question at the centre of [human and LLM co-curation](#c/c-human-curation): who has the final say. Like [ACE](#c/c-ace), it keeps decisions with the human expert and uses the model to reduce effort, the stance behind the survey's [review queue](#c/c-review-queue).

concepts.title: Graphusion
concepts.summary: A 2024 RAG-based method for building knowledge graphs with a global merge step.
concepts.overview: Graphusion (2024) builds knowledge graphs with a retrieval-augmented pipeline and a global merge step that fuses what's extracted from many passages into one graph. It was applied to building concept graphs for the NLP domain. The survey lists it as research worth knowing for anyone building an extraction pipeline: per-passage extraction produces duplicates and conflicts, and a global merge is where they get resolved before a human reviews the result. It relates to [GraphRAG infrastructure](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure) but targets concepts rather than entities.

concepts.title: ProPRL
concepts.summary: A 2026 method for property-aware prerequisite relation learning in educational KGs.
concepts.overview: ProPRL (2026) is a method for learning prerequisite relations in educational knowledge graphs that takes the properties of concepts into account. The survey lists it without further detail. It belongs to the line of work trying to make machine-proposed [prerequisite](#c/c-prerequisite-model) edges more reliable, relevant because [LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges). Better models would raise the quality of proposals entering a human [review queue](#c/c-review-queue), not remove the need for it.

concepts.title: Knowledge gaps from tutor chats via prerequisite graphs
concepts.summary: A 2026 paper that maps student questions onto a prerequisite graph to find missing foundations.
concepts.overview: This 2026 paper extracts a prerequisite graph with GPT-4, then maps the questions students ask a tutor onto it to find the foundations they're missing. It's a use of a [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph) beyond ordering: diagnosing a learner from their questions. It fits the survey's split of responsibilities, where the graph decides *what* a learner needs and an LLM tutor handles *how* ([keep the graph separate from the tutor](#c/c-separate-graph-from-tutor)), and echoes [math-concept-mapper](#c/c-math-concept-mapper)'s class-wide prerequisite-gap dashboard.

concepts.title: LLMs for educational concept and relation extraction
concepts.summary: A 2025 study: few-shot prompting beats zero-shot by ~6 points, and prerequisites gain most.
concepts.overview: This 2025 MDPI study, 'Leveraging LLMs for educational concept and relation extraction', compared prompting strategies. Few-shot prompting beat zero-shot by about 6 points on relation extraction, and prerequisite relations gained the most from examples. It's the evidence for the claim that [few-shot examples improve LLM prerequisite extraction](#c/c-claim-few-shot-helps). For a builder, it suggests a practical step: give the [proposer agent](#c/c-proposer-agent) worked examples of good prerequisite edges, since prerequisites are where LLMs are weakest and where examples help most.

concepts.title: CourseMapper
concepts.summary: RWTH's MOOC platform that extracts concepts from slides and links them to Wikipedia.
concepts.overview: CourseMapper, from RWTH Aachen, is a MOOC platform with educational and personal knowledge graphs. It extracts concepts from course slides and links them to Wikipedia, and its authors found that bottom-up construction, from extracted concepts, beat top-down construction. The survey uses it twice: as the evidence that [bottom-up concept graph construction beats top-down](#c/c-claim-bottom-up-beats-top-down), and as the example of [anchoring concept identity in Wikipedia or Wikidata](#c/c-wikidata-anchoring), part of its advice to [reuse vetted graphs](#c/c-reuse-vetted-graphs) rather than regenerate them.

concepts.title: TutorialBank / LectureBank
concepts.summary: Classic hand-labeled prerequisite datasets used to evaluate prerequisite prediction.
concepts.overview: TutorialBank and LectureBank are classic datasets of concepts with hand-labeled prerequisite relations, used to evaluate how well a method predicts prerequisites. The survey lists them for evaluation: anyone building an LLM pipeline that proposes [prerequisite edges](#c/c-prerequisite-model) needs a ground truth to measure against, as [K12-Bench](#c/c-k12-kgraph) does for K-12 curricula. Measuring against them would show how much a pipeline improves on the ~46–57% baseline before human review.

concepts.title: Systematic review of concept map generation
concepts.summary: A 2025 systematic review of automatic concept-map generation methods.
concepts.overview: This 2025 systematic review surveys methods for generating concept maps automatically. The survey lists it as a starting point for the literature. It's a companion to the specific studies it cites, such as [Graphusion](#c/c-graphusion), [CourseMapper](#c/c-coursemapper) and the [MDPI extraction study](#c/c-mdpi-llm-extraction), and useful context for the [proposer agent](#c/c-proposer-agent) in the suggested stack, whose job is exactly automatic concept-map generation with citations.

concepts.title: Andrej Karpathy
concepts.summary: The AI researcher whose viral 2026 post introduced the LLM Wiki pattern.
concepts.overview: Andrej Karpathy appears in the survey as the author of the [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/c-llm-wiki), described in a viral X post and gist in April 2026. The pattern, raw sources plus an LLM-maintained markdown wiki governed by a schema file and edited by a human in Obsidian, became the most popular human-plus-LLM curation workflow the survey found, with many forks and plugins. The survey's TL;DR places his pattern, alongside Stanford's [Co-STORM](#c/c-co-storm), at the centre of [LLM knowledge curation](#c/c-llm-knowledge-curation).

concepts.title: Knowledge graph
concepts.summary: A graph of concepts or entities joined by typed relations.
concepts.overview: A knowledge graph stores knowledge as nodes (entities or concepts) joined by typed relations, such as 'is part of' or 'was created by'. The survey uses the term in two senses that are worth keeping apart. In [GraphRAG infrastructure](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure), a knowledge graph is extracted from text to help an LLM retrieve facts; its relations describe the world, not the order in which to learn it. A learning graph instead needs [prerequisite](#c/c-prerequisite-graph) relations, 'you need A before B', and nodes that are self-contained learning units. Most of the survey's tools build one kind or the other; the gap it identifies is a tool that builds the second kind with LLM help and human review.

concepts.title: Prerequisite graph
concepts.summary: A concept graph whose edges say 'you need A before B'; the data model the survey is looking for.
concepts.overview: A prerequisite graph splits a subject into well-defined concepts and links them with directed edges meaning 'you need A before B'. It should be a [directed acyclic graph](#c/c-dag), so there is always a [reading order](#c/c-topological-order), and it's what lets a tool compute a [personalized learning plan](#c/c-learning-plan) for any target, as [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy) did. The survey's central finding is that this data model exists in older or tiny projects ([Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy), [Oppia](#c/c-oppia), [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint), [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph)) but is missing from the widely adopted LLM tools, which use outlines, hierarchies or retrieval graphs instead. [The opening](#c/c-the-opening) it recommends is a curated, git-backed prerequisite graph where an agent proposes edges and a human approves them.

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.md: Knowledge split into well-defined chunks (nodes), with edges that say *'you need A before B'*. The rubric wants those edges typed and directed, ideally forming a validated [DAG](#c/c-dag), and not just 'related to' links. Because prerequisite graphs are **DAGs, not trees**, a concept can need several others and unlock several more.

sections.heading: What does it make possible?
sections.md: Pick a target concept and the graph yields every unmet prerequisite in [topological order](#c/c-topological-order): [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy)'s [personalized learning plan](#c/c-learning-plan). It drives review too: [Oppia](#c/c-oppia) lessons declare prerequisite skills that trigger review questions at the start of a lesson. With a mastery model on top, practice can flow credit back to prerequisites ([encompassing edges](#c/c-encompassing-edges), as in [Math Academy](#c/c-math-academy)), and a tutor can find a student's missing foundations by mapping their questions onto the graph, as one 2026 paper does with tutor chats.

sections.heading: Who has one today?
sections.md: The [prerequisite-graph learning systems](#c/c-prerequisite-graph-learning-systems) have the right data model: [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy) (archived), [Oppia](#c/c-oppia), [Learning Commons](#c/c-learning-commons-kg) for K-12 data, [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint) for formal math, and [small DAG engines](#c/c-small-dag-engines) such as [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph) and [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder). They have little LLM co-authoring and weak visualization. The popular LLM tools, [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor) and [OpenMAIC](#c/c-openmaic), have no explicit, curatable prerequisite graph, and [GraphRAG](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure) graphs don't model 'learn A before B' at all.

sections.heading: How should one be built?
sections.md: The survey's recipe: keep one markdown file per concept with `requires` and `helps` in frontmatter ([plain files plus git](#c/c-files-plus-git)); let an agent [propose edges with confidence and evidence](#c/c-edge-proposals); send doubtful ones to a [review queue](#c/c-review-queue); check for cycles in CI; and [reuse vetted graphs](#c/c-reuse-vetted-graphs) such as Learning Commons where they exist. Draw it [DAG-first](#c/c-dag-first-visualization), with a [layered layout](#c/c-layered-layout).

sections.heading: How is it different from a knowledge graph or a mind map?
sections.md: A general [knowledge graph](#c/c-knowledge-graph), like those built by GraphRAG tools, records facts about entities; its edges say how things relate in the world, not what to learn first. A mind map, like Co-STORM's or NotebookLM's, is a hierarchy of subtopics: it shows how a subject breaks down but can't give a concept two parents. A prerequisite graph is narrower than the first and more general than the second. Its only essential edge is 'you need A before B', and it's a DAG, so the same foundation can feed many later concepts. That narrowness is what makes it useful for ordering a learner's path, and also what makes its edges hard for an LLM to get right.

concepts.title: Directed acyclic graph
concepts.summary: A graph of one-way edges with no cycles, so every node can be reached in some order.
concepts.overview: A directed acyclic graph, or DAG, is a graph whose edges point one way and never loop back. That property is exactly what a [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph) needs: if A requires B and B requires A, no learner can start. The survey stresses that prerequisite graphs are **DAGs, not trees**, since a concept can have several prerequisites and unlock several others, which is why tree-shaped mind-map tools like [markmap](#c/c-markmap) can't represent them. A DAG always has a [topological order](#c/c-topological-order), the basis of a [learning plan](#c/c-learning-plan), and it's best drawn with a [layered layout](#c/c-layered-layout). Keeping a hand-edited graph acyclic takes [CI checks for cycles](#c/c-ci-graph-checks), as PathFinder and OpenScienceBasedLearningPlatform do.

concepts.title: Topological order
concepts.summary: An ordering of a DAG that puts every prerequisite before whatever depends on it.
concepts.overview: A topological order lists the nodes of a [directed acyclic graph](#c/c-dag) so that every edge points forward: each prerequisite comes before the concepts that need it. It's the algorithm behind [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy)'s [personalized learning plan](#c/c-learning-plan), which takes a target concept, collects all its unmet prerequisites and presents them in topological order. Any DAG has at least one such order, and usually many; a cycle makes one impossible, which is why file-based prerequisite graphs need [CI checks for cycles](#c/c-ci-graph-checks). The same ordering idea powers [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything)'s [dependency-ordered guided tours](#c/c-guided-tour) over a codebase.

concepts.title: Personalized learning plan
concepts.summary: Every unmet prerequisite of a chosen target, in reading order, with curated resources.
concepts.overview: A personalized learning plan is what [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy) computed: pick a target concept, and it returns all the prerequisites you haven't met, in [topological order](#c/c-topological-order), each with curated resources and time estimates. It's the clearest demonstration of why a [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph) is worth building, and the survey's design section returns to it as the core learner view: a layered 'what do I need first?' view for one target (see [DAG-first visualization](#c/c-dag-first-visualization)). The suggested learner UI keeps it as a 'plan my path to X' action. Adding [mastery tracking](#c/c-mastery-tracking) would let the plan drop what a learner already knows.

concepts.title: Curation bottleneck
concepts.summary: Hand-writing every node and edge doesn't scale; it's what sank Metacademy.
concepts.overview: The curation bottleneck is the survey's name for why hand-built prerequisite graphs stall: experts have to write every node and every edge by hand, and there are never enough expert hours. It was [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy)'s downfall, despite the survey calling its design the cleanest statement of the idea. LLM-assisted curation is meant to fix exactly that, but LLMs alone make too many prerequisite mistakes, so the fix is a middle path: models propose, and humans confirm the edges that matter, as in [ACE](#c/c-ace), which cut expert effort a lot. Keeping content in [plain files plus git](#c/c-files-plus-git) spreads the remaining work across contributors.

concepts.title: Skill as learning unit
concepts.summary: Oppia's learning unit: a skill phrased 'given X, compute Y', with examples and misconceptions.
concepts.overview: The survey singles out [Oppia](#c/c-oppia)'s skill as a proven answer to 'how big should a node be?'. A skill is phrased as a task, 'given X, compute Y', and carries a concept card, worked examples and the misconceptions learners typically have. That phrasing makes a node testable, which matters for [mastery tracking](#c/c-mastery-tracking), and small enough to have clear [prerequisites](#c/c-prerequisite-model). It's the survey's model for [chunked nodes](#c/c-chunked-nodes), the 'well-defined chunks' of the first pillar, and a counterweight to the vaguer topic-sized nodes that mind maps and wikis produce.

concepts.title: Mastery tracking
concepts.summary: Estimating what a learner has mastered, so the graph can decide what comes next.
concepts.overview: Mastery tracking estimates which concepts a learner has mastered, so a system can skip what they know and choose what's next. It's what the rubric calls [learner state](#c/c-learner-state). The survey's position is that mastery should come from a transparent model, not from an LLM's judgment: [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/c-bkt), as in [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder) and [Oppia](#c/c-oppia), or Math Academy-style [encompassing credit](#c/c-encompassing-edges), where practice on an advanced topic counts as review of its prerequisites. [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph) adds a level to it: a definition doesn't satisfy a dependency that needs a calculation. In the proposed product, mastery shows as a [mastery overlay](#c/c-mastery-overlay) on the graph.

sections.heading: What is it for?
sections.md: The rubric's *learner state* criterion asks for mastery tracking and a personalized path through the graph. Knowing what a learner has mastered lets a [learning plan](#c/c-learning-plan) skip it, lets a tutor pick the next node, and lets a map show progress.

sections.heading: How do the tools do it?
sections.md: [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder) estimates mastery with [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/c-bkt) and redoes the plan when quiz scores come in. [Oppia](#c/c-oppia) pairs prerequisite skills with BKT and is the survey's model for learner modeling. [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor) offers mastery paths with progression gates and a three-layer learner memory. The open-source propositional-logic 'Math Academy' gives [fractional credit](#c/c-encompassing-edges) to prerequisite topics, weighted by edge weight, when a problem is solved. [Cognitive-knowledge-graph-engine](#c/c-cognitive-kg-engine) combines a prerequisite-aware graph with mastery tracking and recommendations.

sections.heading: Why not let the LLM judge?
sections.md: The survey says mastery should come from a transparent model, BKT or Math Academy-style credit that flows to prerequisites, not from LLM judgment. That fits its larger point that the curated graph decides *what* to learn and an LLM tutor handles *how*: see [keep the graph separate from the tutor](#c/c-separate-graph-from-tutor).

sections.heading: Mastery has levels
sections.md: [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph) notes that 'a definition doesn't satisfy a dependency that needs a calculation'. The design section turns this into [depth-qualified prerequisites](#c/c-depth-qualified-prerequisites): an edge can require B at the *apply* level, not just *define*. A mastery model would then track level per concept, not a single yes or no.

sections.heading: How does it change what the learner sees?
sections.md: Without mastery tracking, a learning plan lists every prerequisite of a target, including ones the learner already knows well, which makes paths look long and discouraging. With it, known concepts drop out and the path shrinks to what's actually missing. The survey wants this visible: its learner view overlays mastery on the graph, and its proposed product has 'learners explore a zoomable graph with mastery overlays'. Diagnostic placement, which Math Academy uses to find where a learner starts, is the complement: it seeds the mastery model so a new learner doesn't have to prove everything from scratch.

sections.heading: What goes wrong without a transparent model?
sections.md: An opaque mastery judgment can't be questioned. If a system decides a learner has mastered a topic because an LLM said so, neither the learner nor a teacher can see why, or correct it when it's wrong. A probabilistic model like BKT, or explicit credit flowing along encompassing edges, can be inspected: each estimate traces back to specific answers. That transparency is the same principle the survey applies to prerequisite edges, where every proposal should carry its evidence.

concepts.title: Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
concepts.summary: A transparent probabilistic model that updates a learner's mastery estimate from each answer.
concepts.overview: Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) models each skill as known or not known and updates the probability that a learner knows it after every answer, allowing for lucky guesses and careless slips. In the survey it's the recommended way to do [mastery tracking](#c/c-mastery-tracking), because it's transparent: you can see why the system thinks a skill is mastered. [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder) uses BKT to estimate mastery and replan when quiz scores arrive, and [Oppia](#c/c-oppia)-style prerequisite skills plus BKT are named the best model to copy for learner modeling. The design section pairs it with Math Academy-style [encompassing credit](#c/c-encompassing-edges) as the alternatives to letting an LLM decide what a learner knows.

concepts.title: Encompassing edges
concepts.summary: Practising an advanced topic gives implicit review credit to the prerequisites it encompasses.
concepts.overview: Encompassing edges come from [Math Academy](#c/c-math-academy): when an advanced topic encompasses a simpler one, practising the advanced topic gives implicit review credit to its prerequisites. Review happens as a side effect of moving forward. The open-source [propositional-logic clone](#c/c-propositional-logic-math-academy) implements a version, giving fractional credit to prerequisite topics weighted by edge weight. The survey adopts `encompasses` as one of its [edge types](#c/c-edge-types) and names prerequisite credit, alongside [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/c-bkt), as the kind of transparent model [mastery tracking](#c/c-mastery-tracking) should use instead of LLM judgment.

concepts.title: Node status roll-up
concepts.summary: Each small node has a status, and overall progress is just the sum of node statuses.
concepts.overview: In [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint), every node, a definition or theorem, carries a status: not ready, ready or formalized. Because nodes are small and locally specified, many humans and AI agents can work on different nodes at once, and global progress is simply a roll-up of node statuses, visible as colours on the dependency graph. The survey calls this the collaboration pattern a learning graph wants. It reappears in the [suggested starting stack](#c/c-starting-stack) as a `status: proposed|reviewed` field in each concept file, so the graph shows at a glance how much of it a human has checked.

concepts.title: Dependency-ordered guided tour
concepts.summary: A walk through a graph in dependency order, built by an LLM from the graph.
concepts.overview: A dependency-ordered guided tour is how [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything) teaches a codebase: a tour-builder agent walks the learner through the architecture so that each part is introduced after the parts it depends on. The survey treats it as the UX reference for 'LLM builds a graph, then gives a guided tour'. For general knowledge, the same experience is a [learning plan](#c/c-learning-plan) walked in [topological order](#c/c-topological-order) over a [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph); the difference is that the dependencies must be proposed and verified rather than parsed from code.

concepts.title: Critic agent
concepts.summary: An independent agent that checks the generated graph for cycles, missing prerequisites and weak evidence.
concepts.overview: A critic, or graph-reviewer, agent reviews what the proposer produced before a human sees it. [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph) uses an independent critic model to review its graph, and [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything)'s pipeline has a separate graph-reviewer agent that the survey says is worth copying. In the [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack), the critic checks for cycles, finds missing prerequisites and verifies evidence. It complements, rather than replaces, the human [review queue](#c/c-review-queue): an independent pass catches mechanical and obvious errors cheaply, so human attention goes to the judgment calls.

concepts.title: Proposer agent
concepts.summary: The agent that extracts concepts and prerequisite edges from sources, with citations.
concepts.overview: In the survey's [suggested starting stack](#c/c-starting-stack), the proposer agent reads sources and extracts concepts and edges, each with citations, producing the [proposals](#c/c-edge-proposals) that humans review. It's the LLM's main job in the curation half of the system. The research suggests how to make it better: give it few-shot examples, since [they help prerequisites most](#c/c-claim-few-shot-helps), and build bottom-up from the sources, as [CourseMapper](#c/c-coursemapper) found works better. Its output then passes through the [critic agent](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent) and the [review queue](#c/c-review-queue).

concepts.title: Tutor agent
concepts.summary: The agent that writes per-node explanations and quizzes for the learner.
concepts.overview: The tutor agent is the third agent in the survey's [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack): it writes per-node explanations and quizzes. It embodies the rule to [keep the graph separate from the tutor](#c/c-separate-graph-from-tutor): the curated graph decides what the learner studies next, and the tutor, DeepTutor- or OpenMAIC-style, decides how to teach that one node. Its quiz results can feed a transparent mastery model such as [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/c-bkt), as in PathFinder, rather than the tutor judging mastery itself.

concepts.title: Evidence-cited edges
concepts.summary: Every concept and edge cites the passage in the sources that supports it.
concepts.overview: In [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph), every concept and prerequisite edge cites evidence from the source texts. The survey names this the model for evidence-backed LLM extraction and builds it into its first design rule: each [proposed edge](#c/c-edge-proposals) carries cited evidence along with a confidence score. Evidence makes review fast, since a curator checks a quote rather than re-deriving the subject, and it lets a [critic agent](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent) verify that an edge is actually supported. [Graphify](#c/c-graphify)'s 'every edge explained' is a looser version of the same idea.

concepts.title: Edges as proposals with confidence
concepts.summary: Every AI-made prerequisite edge is a proposal with a confidence score and cited evidence until reviewed.
concepts.overview: The survey's first design implication: make every AI-made prerequisite edge a proposal, not a fact. Each carries a confidence score and [cited evidence](#c/c-evidence-cited-edges) from the sources, the SyllabusGraph pattern. Low-confidence or high-impact edges go to a [human review queue](#c/c-review-queue), the ACE pattern, and the system records who approved what. Until reviewed, proposed edges are drawn in a distinct style so learners can tell them apart. This is the survey's answer to two facts at once: [LLMs are unreliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges), and hand-writing every edge hits the [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck).

sections.heading: What is proposed?
sections.md: Every prerequisite edge an agent creates starts life as a **proposal**, carrying a **confidence score** and **cited evidence** from the sources. The opening described in the TL;DR is built around it: an agent *proposes* nodes and prerequisite edges with evidence and confidence, and a human accepts or rejects them.

sections.heading: Why not trust the model's edges?
sections.md: Because prerequisite edges are where LLMs are weakest and where errors cost the most. Frontier models score only ~46–57% exact match on K12-Bench prerequisite reasoning, and a missing or backwards prerequisite sends learners into material they can't yet follow. See [LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges) and [prerequisite errors cost learners the most](#c/c-claim-prereq-errors-costly).

sections.heading: Where do the pieces come from?
sections.md: The evidence requirement comes from [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph), where every concept and edge cites the source texts and an independent critic model reviews the graph. The routing comes from [ACE](#c/c-ace), which sends only top-ranked candidate edges to experts. In the [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack), a [proposer agent](#c/c-proposer-agent) writes the proposals, a [critic](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent) checks them for cycles, missing prerequisites and unsupported evidence, and concept files carry `status: proposed|reviewed` and `confidence` in their frontmatter.

sections.heading: What happens after review?
sections.md: Low-confidence or high-impact edges go to a [human review queue](#c/c-review-queue); the rest can be accepted with lighter checks. The system **records who approved what**, which with git-backed files means commits carry the provenance. In the learner's view, [AI-proposed edges that haven't been reviewed yet are marked in a distinct style](#c/c-dag-first-visualization), so nobody mistakes a guess for curated structure.

sections.heading: What does a proposal look like in practice?
sections.md: In the suggested stack's concept files, a proposal is simply a `requires` or `helps` entry in a concept's frontmatter while its `status` is `proposed`, with a `confidence` value and `sources` citing the passages it came from. Accepting it means changing the status to `reviewed` in a commit. Because the files live in git, the full history of every edge (who proposed it, what evidence it cited, who approved it and when) is available without a separate database. It's worth considering making status and confidence per edge rather than per concept, since one concept may have some reviewed and some proposed prerequisites; the survey's stack puts them at the file level.

concepts.title: Human review queue
concepts.summary: A queue where a human accepts or rejects AI-proposed edges, starting with uncertain or high-impact ones.
concepts.overview: The review queue is where [human curation](#c/c-human-curation) happens in the survey's design. AI-proposed edges, each with [confidence and cited evidence](#c/c-edge-proposals), arrive in a queue; a human accepts or rejects them, and the system records who approved what. Low-confidence or high-impact edges are routed there first, the pattern of [ACE](#c/c-ace), which the survey calls the blueprint for the review queue and which [cut expert effort while improving learning orders](#c/c-claim-human-review-cuts-effort). In the [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack) it lives in a React Flow [curation UI](#c/c-curation-ui), and git commits record the provenance. It's the heart of [the opening](#c/c-the-opening).

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.md: A queue of AI-proposed nodes and prerequisite edges that a human **accepts or rejects**. The survey's TL;DR puts it at the centre of the opening it identifies: an agent proposes, a human accepts or rejects in a review queue.

sections.heading: What goes into it, and in what order?
sections.md: Every edge arrives as a [proposal](#c/c-edge-proposals) with a confidence score and cited evidence. **Low-confidence or high-impact edges** are routed to the human queue. [ACE](#c/c-ace) is the blueprint: it scores concept pairs, sends the top-ranked candidates to experts, and infers further edges from what they confirm, which cut expert effort a lot and produced learning orders that improved student success.

sections.heading: Why is it necessary?
sections.md: Because [LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges) (~46–57% exact match on K12-Bench) and [prerequisite errors cost learners the most](#c/c-claim-prereq-errors-costly). Without review, a learning graph is a guess; with review of everything, it's the [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck) again. A ranked queue is the middle path.

sections.heading: How is it built?
sections.md: In the [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack), the [curation UI](#c/c-curation-ui) is a **React Flow editor with an accept/reject queue** for proposed edges, and **git commits record provenance**. Each concept file carries `status: proposed|reviewed` and `confidence`. The [critic agent](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent) runs before the queue, checking for cycles, missing prerequisites and unsupported evidence, so the human sees cleaner proposals.

sections.heading: What should a reviewer see for each item?
sections.md: Enough to decide quickly: the two concepts, the proposed edge type (hard or soft prerequisite, part-of, encompasses), the confidence, the cited passages, and anything the critic flagged, such as a would-be cycle. With evidence attached, a reviewer is checking a claim against a quote rather than recalling the whole subject. Accepted and rejected decisions should both be kept: rejections are useful examples for the proposer's few-shot prompts, which the MDPI study found help prerequisites most.

concepts.title: Distinct prerequisite edge types
concepts.summary: Separate requires, helps, part-of, related and encompasses edges instead of one generic link.
concepts.overview: The survey's second design implication is to distinguish edge types rather than treat every link as 'related'. It proposes five: `requires`, a [hard prerequisite](#c/c-hard-prerequisite); `helps`, a [soft prerequisite](#c/c-soft-prerequisite); `part-of`, for decomposition; `related`; and `encompasses`, Math Academy-style [implicit practice](#c/c-encompassing-edges). It also suggests [depth-qualified prerequisites](#c/c-depth-qualified-prerequisites). Types let a learning plan be strict about what's truly required and lenient about what merely helps. [Skillgraph_OS](#c/c-skillgraph-os) already separates prerequisite and helps-with edges, and the suggested concept files hold `requires` and `helps` in frontmatter.

concepts.title: Hard prerequisite (requires)
concepts.summary: A 'requires' edge: you can't learn B without first learning A.
concepts.overview: A hard prerequisite, the `requires` edge in the survey's proposed [edge types](#c/c-edge-types), means B can't be learned without A. It's the edge that defines a learning plan's order and the one where [errors cost learners the most](#c/c-claim-prereq-errors-costly), so it's the main target of human review. [Obsidian + Breadcrumbs](#c/c-obsidian-breadcrumbs) can express it as a custom `requires` link, and the suggested concept files hold it in a `requires:` frontmatter field. It contrasts with the [soft prerequisite](#c/c-soft-prerequisite), and can be sharpened into a [depth-qualified prerequisite](#c/c-depth-qualified-prerequisites).

concepts.title: Soft prerequisite (helps)
concepts.summary: A 'helps' edge: knowing A makes B easier, but isn't required.
concepts.overview: A soft prerequisite, the `helps` edge in the survey's [edge types](#c/c-edge-types), says that knowing A makes B easier without being strictly necessary. Separating it from a [hard prerequisite](#c/c-hard-prerequisite) keeps learning plans short, since only hard edges must be satisfied, while still pointing learners to useful background. [Skillgraph_OS](#c/c-skillgraph-os) already distinguishes 'prerequisite' from 'helps-with' edges and offers alternative routes through the graph, and the suggested concept files carry a `helps` field next to `requires`.

concepts.title: Depth-qualified prerequisites
concepts.summary: Prerequisites that name a level: 'requires B at the apply level, not just define'.
concepts.overview: A depth-qualified prerequisite says not just that B is needed, but how well: 'requires B at the *apply* level, not just *define*'. The survey suggests considering them, noting that [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph) hints at the idea with its rule that 'a definition doesn't satisfy a dependency that needs a calculation'. They'd make a [hard prerequisite](#c/c-hard-prerequisite) more precise and pair naturally with level-aware [mastery tracking](#c/c-mastery-tracking), so a learner who can state a definition isn't sent on to material that needs them to use it.

concepts.title: Plain files plus git
concepts.summary: One markdown file per concept, with prerequisites in frontmatter, versioned and reviewed in git.
concepts.overview: The survey's third design implication is to keep a learning graph in plain files under git rather than a database: one markdown file per concept, with frontmatter for prerequisites, objectives, resources and checks. Agents and humans edit the same files, review happens in diffs or pull requests, and [CI checks for cycles and dangling references](#c/c-ci-graph-checks) keep the graph valid. The survey's reason is that [every successful curated-knowledge project it found works this way](#c/c-claim-files-git-beats-db): [roadmap.sh](#c/c-roadmap-sh), Learn Anything, [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint), the [LLM Wiki](#c/c-llm-wiki) and Understand-Anything's committed JSON. It's the storage layer of [the opening](#c/c-the-opening).

sections.heading: What's the recommendation?
sections.md: **Plain files plus git beats a database for curation.** Keep one markdown file per concept, with frontmatter for prerequisites, objectives, resources and checks. Agents and humans edit the same files, and review happens in diffs or pull requests. Add CI checks for cycles and dangling references, as [OpenScienceBasedLearningPlatform](#c/c-openscience-platform) does.

sections.heading: What's the evidence?
sections.md: Every successful curated-knowledge project the survey found keeps content in files under version control. [roadmap.sh](#c/c-roadmap-sh) stores each node as `content/<topic>@<node-id>.md` and takes community PRs at the scale of ~368k★. [Learn Anything](#c/c-learn-anything) worked the same way. [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint) lives in the formalization repo. The [LLM Wiki](#c/c-llm-wiki) is plain markdown plus git. [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything) commits its graph as JSON. This is a pattern across examples, not a controlled comparison.

sections.heading: Why does it suit human-plus-agent curation?
sections.md: Files are the one format both sides already work in. An agent proposes a change as a diff; a human reviews it as a pull request; git records who approved what, which is the provenance the survey asks for. The DIY route shows how little it takes: one note per concept with a `requires:` field, an agent that proposes notes and edges reviewed through git diffs, and a graph view, about 70% of the vision in a weekend for one user.

sections.heading: What does it look like in the suggested stack?
sections.md: A folder of `concepts/*.md` files whose frontmatter holds `requires`, `helps`, `objectives`, `sources`, `status: proposed|reviewed` and `confidence` ([concept files](#c/c-concept-files)). The [curation UI](#c/c-curation-ui) is a React Flow editor whose accept/reject decisions become git commits, so the history of the graph is the history of the repo.

sections.heading: What are the trade-offs?
sections.md: Files make some things harder. Queries across the whole graph ('everything that requires X') need an index built from the files. Concurrent edits can conflict, and a merge conflict in frontmatter is less friendly than a database transaction. And integrity isn't enforced by a schema, which is why the survey pairs files with CI checks for cycles and dangling references. The survey judges the curation benefits worth it: shared editing by agents and people, review in diffs, and provenance from commit history.

concepts.title: CI checks for cycles and dangling references
concepts.summary: Automated checks that reject changes introducing prerequisite cycles or broken references.
concepts.overview: When a learning graph lives in [plain files under git](#c/c-files-plus-git), anyone, human or agent, can break it with one edit. The survey's fix, borrowed from [OpenScienceBasedLearningPlatform](#c/c-openscience-platform), is to run CI checks on every change: no duplicate IDs, no references to concepts that don't exist, and no prerequisite cycles, so the graph stays a valid [DAG](#c/c-dag). [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder) similarly validates its NetworkX skill graph for cycles. In the suggested stack, the [critic agent](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent) also checks for cycles, catching problems before they reach review.

concepts.title: Keep the graph separate from the tutor
concepts.summary: The curated graph decides what to learn and in what order; an LLM tutor decides how to teach it.
concepts.overview: The survey's fourth design implication splits responsibilities. The curated [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph) decides *what* to learn and in what order. An LLM [tutor](#c/c-tutor-agent), in the style of [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor) or OpenMAIC, handles *how*: generating explanations and quizzes for one node at a time. Mastery comes from a [transparent model](#c/c-claim-transparent-mastery), not LLM judgment. The split puts each part where it's reliable: structure, where LLMs are weak, is curated by people; teaching, where LLMs are strong, is generated. It also means the survey can reuse the hugely adopted AI tutors instead of competing with them.

sections.heading: What's the split?
sections.md: **Keep the graph separate from the tutor.** The curated DAG decides *what* to learn and in what order. An LLM tutor, DeepTutor- or OpenMAIC-style, handles *how*, generating explanations and quizzes for one node at a time. Mastery should come from a transparent model ([BKT](#c/c-bkt) or Math Academy-style credit that flows to prerequisites), not from LLM judgment.

sections.heading: Why split them?
sections.md: Because the two jobs have opposite reliability profiles. LLMs are [unreliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges), so the structure needs human curation. They're good at explaining and quizzing, which is where the [AI tutors](#c/c-ai-tutors) already shine. Joining them in one LLM, as today's tutors do with their opaque 'mastery paths', leaves the order uninspectable and uncorrectable.

sections.heading: Where does it come from?
sections.md: From the survey's reading of [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor): the strongest open-source LLM tutor foundation, which you could pair with a curated concept DAG, so that the graph decides *what's next* and DeepTutor-style agents *teach it*. [OpenMAIC](#c/c-openmaic)'s editable outline shows a similar separation between a human-curated plan and agent-generated lessons.

sections.heading: How does it show up in the stack?
sections.md: The [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack) has a separate [tutor agent](#c/c-tutor-agent) for per-node explanations and quizzes, distinct from the [proposer](#c/c-proposer-agent) and [critic](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent) that build the graph. The [learner UI](#c/c-learner-ui) shows the graph with a mastery overlay and 'plan my path to X'; the tutor takes over once a node is chosen.

sections.heading: What does each side need from the other?
sections.md: The tutor needs the node it's teaching and that node's context: its prerequisites, which the learner has presumably mastered, and its objectives and sources from the concept file. The graph needs the tutor's evidence about the learner, quiz results that feed the mastery model. Keeping this interface narrow is what makes the tutor swappable: DeepTutor, OpenMAIC or a simple per-node prompt could all sit on the same curated graph. It also keeps the graph reusable beyond one tutor, as Learning Commons' data is reusable through its MCP server.

concepts.title: DAG-first visualization
concepts.summary: A layered 'what do I need first?' view for one target, zoomable to a whole-field map with mastery shown.
concepts.overview: The survey's fifth design implication is that visualization should be DAG-first. Start with a layered 'what do I need first?' view for one target concept, like [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy)'s [learning plan](#c/c-learning-plan), and let the learner zoom out to a whole-field map at [Sigma.js](#c/c-sigma-js) scale. Overlay [mastery](#c/c-mastery-overlay), and draw AI-proposed edges that haven't been reviewed in a distinct style. It rests on the claim that [layered layouts beat force-directed ones](#c/c-claim-layered-beats-force) for prerequisites, since prerequisite graphs are DAGs, not trees. The suggested [learner UI](#c/c-learner-ui) implements it with Cytoscape.js or Sigma.js and a dagre or ELK layout.

sections.heading: What does the learner see?
sections.md: First, a **layered 'what do I need first?' view for one target concept**: the target and its prerequisites, foundations at the bottom and the goal at the top, in the manner of [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy)'s learning plan. From there the view **zooms out to a whole-field map**, at the scale of thousands of nodes that [Sigma.js](#c/c-sigma-js) handles.

sections.heading: Why layered, not force-directed?
sections.md: Prerequisite graphs are **DAGs, not trees**, so tree-shaped mind maps can't show them, and a [layered (Sugiyama) layout](#c/c-layered-layout) reads far better than a [force-directed](#c/c-force-directed-layout) one for 'what do I need first?'. Layer engines like [dagre and ELK](#c/c-dagre-elk) compute it for React Flow and Cytoscape.js.

sections.heading: What goes on top of the graph?
sections.md: Two overlays. A [mastery overlay](#c/c-mastery-overlay) shows what the learner already knows, so the path visibly shrinks. And **AI-proposed edges that haven't been reviewed** are marked in a distinct style, so learners can tell curated structure from suggestions, which matters since [LLMs are unreliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges).

sections.heading: How does it fit the product?
sections.md: It's the learner half of [the opening](#c/c-the-opening): learners explore a zoomable graph with mastery overlays. In the [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack), the [learner UI](#c/c-learner-ui) is Cytoscape.js or Sigma.js with a dagre or ELK layered layout, a mastery overlay and 'plan my path to X'. The curation half is a separate editable view built on React Flow.

sections.heading: What should curators see differently?
sections.md: Curators need the same graph with a different emphasis: every proposed edge, its confidence and its evidence, and a queue of what's waiting. That's why the survey puts curation in a separate [React Flow](#c/c-react-flow) editor, which is built for editing nodes and edges, rather than in the learner's map. The two views share one underlying graph, and the distinct style for unreviewed edges in the learner's view is how the curation state leaks through, honestly, to learners.

concepts.title: Layered (Sugiyama) layout
concepts.summary: A graph layout in layers, foundations at the bottom and goals at the top.
concepts.overview: A layered layout, also called Sugiyama layout, arranges a [DAG](#c/c-dag) in horizontal layers so every edge points the same way: foundations at the bottom, goals at the top. The survey says it reads far better than [force-directed layouts](#c/c-force-directed-layout) for the learner's real question, 'what do I need first?'. Libraries such as [dagre and ELK](#c/c-dagre-elk) compute it, and they plug into [React Flow](#c/c-react-flow) for editing and [Cytoscape.js](#c/c-cytoscape-js) for viewing. It's the layout behind the recommended [DAG-first visualization](#c/c-dag-first-visualization) and the [learner UI](#c/c-learner-ui) in the suggested stack.

concepts.title: Force-directed layout
concepts.summary: A physics-style graph layout where linked nodes pull together and others push apart.
concepts.overview: A force-directed layout treats edges as springs and nodes as charges, letting the graph settle into clusters. It's the default in many graph tools, including [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything)'s interactive codebase graph, and it's good at showing what belongs together. The survey argues it's the wrong default for learning: a force-directed picture of a [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph) hides the direction of dependency, so a learner can't read 'what do I need first?' off it. A [layered layout](#c/c-layered-layout), with foundations at the bottom and goals at the top, reads far better for that question.

concepts.title: Mastery overlay
concepts.summary: Colouring the concept graph by what the learner has already mastered.
concepts.overview: A mastery overlay colours the concept graph by what the learner has mastered, so they can see their progress and how much of a path remains. The survey includes it in [the opening](#c/c-the-opening), in the [DAG-first visualization](#c/c-dag-first-visualization) design rule, and in the suggested [learner UI](#c/c-learner-ui). It depends on [mastery tracking](#c/c-mastery-tracking) from a transparent model such as [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/c-bkt). Similar ideas already exist in small form: [niyue/skillmap](#c/c-niyue-skillmap) draws progress bars on a skill tree, and Lean Blueprint colours nodes by status.

concepts.title: Reuse vetted graphs
concepts.summary: Import existing curated graphs where they exist instead of generating new ones.
concepts.overview: The survey's sixth design implication: reuse, don't regenerate, where vetted graphs exist. [Learning Commons](#c/c-learning-commons-kg) covers K-12 standards and progressions and has an MCP server. Mathlib and blueprint dependency graphs cover formal math. Wikipedia and Wikidata can [anchor concept identity](#c/c-wikidata-anchoring), as CourseMapper does. Given that [LLMs are unreliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges), an expert-built skeleton is worth more than a generated one, and it lightens the [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck). In the suggested stack, Learning Commons is the K-12 [seed data](#c/c-seed-data).

concepts.title: Wikipedia/Wikidata concept anchoring
concepts.summary: Linking each concept to a Wikipedia or Wikidata entry to pin down its identity.
concepts.overview: Concept identity is a quiet problem in any extracted graph: two sources name the same idea differently, or one name covers two ideas. The survey suggests anchoring concepts to Wikipedia or Wikidata, as [CourseMapper](#c/c-coursemapper) does when it links concepts extracted from slides to Wikipedia. An anchor gives each concept a stable, shared identity, helps merge duplicates, and connects the graph to a vetted external source. It's part of the survey's advice to [reuse vetted graphs](#c/c-reuse-vetted-graphs) rather than regenerate everything.

concepts.title: Distribute as an agent skill or MCP server
concepts.summary: Ship the curation tool as a skill for coding agents, or an MCP server, plus a static viewer.
concepts.overview: The survey's seventh design implication is about distribution. [Graphify](#c/c-graphify) and [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything) reached massive adoption by shipping as skills for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, so a 'curate a concept graph' skill plus a static viewer is a low-friction way in. An [MCP server](#c/c-mcp-server) is the other route, the one Learning Commons already takes for its data. The approach fits the rest of the design: a skill produces [plain files](#c/c-files-plus-git) in the user's repo, and a static viewer, like Understand-Anything's no-LLM viewer, displays them. The evidence is the [adoption of those two tools](#c/c-claim-skills-drive-adoption).

concepts.title: MCP server
concepts.summary: A standard interface that lets AI agents call a tool or dataset directly.
concepts.overview: An MCP (Model Context Protocol) server exposes a tool or dataset to AI agents in a standard way. It comes up twice in the survey. [Learning Commons](#c/c-learning-commons-kg) ships one, which makes its vetted K-12 prerequisite data directly usable by agents, and llm-wiki-kit packages the LLM Wiki pattern as one. And the design section recommends [distributing a curation tool as an agent skill or MCP server](#c/c-agent-skill-distribution), the route that gave Graphify and Understand-Anything their adoption: a 'curate a concept graph' skill plus a static viewer.

concepts.title: Human edits the plan, then agents generate
concepts.summary: A human edits the outline first, then agents generate the content from it.
concepts.overview: In [OpenMAIC](#c/c-openmaic), generation runs from an outline to scenes, and the outline is editable by a human before anything else is generated. 'Edit with AI' applies validated JSON-patch edits to it. The survey singles this out as a reference pattern: the human curates the plan, cheap to review and decisive for quality, and agents do the expensive generation afterwards. The outline-editing step is the curation hook. For a learning graph, the equivalent plan is the [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph) itself, reviewed through a [review queue](#c/c-review-queue) before a [tutor agent](#c/c-tutor-agent) writes lessons for each node.

concepts.title: Committed JSON graph
concepts.summary: The graph is committed to the repo as JSON, so teams share it and a viewer needs no LLM.
concepts.overview: [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything) commits its generated graph to the repository as a JSON file. Teams then share one graph through git, changes show up in diffs, and a read-only viewer can display it without running an LLM. The survey names it as worth copying and counts it among the projects showing that [plain files plus git](#c/c-files-plus-git) beat a database for curation: agents and humans edit the same files, and review happens in diffs or pull requests.

concepts.title: Dynamic mind map
concepts.summary: Co-STORM's evolving concept hierarchy, shared between the human and the AI agents.
concepts.overview: In [Co-STORM](#c/c-co-storm), the dynamic mind map is a hierarchical concept structure that the system updates as a discussion between a human and AI agents unfolds. It serves as a shared conceptual space: both sides can see how the topic is being organized. The survey values the idea of a structure that human and machine build together, but notes its limit: a mind map is a hierarchy, a tree of subtopics, and so it can't express a [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph), which is a [DAG](#c/c-dag). The same limit applies to NotebookLM's and Khoj's generated mind maps.

concepts.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
concepts.summary: An LLM answers from passages retrieved from a document collection.
concepts.overview: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets an LLM answer from your own material: it retrieves relevant passages from a corpus and puts them in the prompt. It's the backbone of the [AI tutors](#c/c-ai-tutors); [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor) runs RAG over your materials through LlamaIndex, [GraphRAG](#c/c-microsoft-graphrag) and [LightRAG](#c/c-lightrag). GraphRAG variants add a [knowledge graph](#c/c-knowledge-graph) of entities and relations to improve retrieval. That's why the survey keeps separating two kinds of graph: in DeepTutor, knowledge graphs are used *inside retrieval*, and there's no curated, learner-visible prerequisite graph. The [GraphRAG infrastructure](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure) tools are useful as an ingestion layer that finds candidate concepts, not as the teaching graph.

concepts.title: The opening: a curated, git-backed concept DAG
concepts.summary: A local-first, git-backed concept DAG where agents propose, humans review and learners explore; nothing fills it yet.
concepts.overview: The opening is the survey's name for the gap in the landscape: a local-first, git-backed concept DAG where an agent *proposes* nodes and prerequisite edges with evidence and confidence, a human accepts or rejects them in a [review queue](#c/c-review-queue), and learners explore a zoomable graph with [mastery overlays](#c/c-mastery-overlay). It combines the pieces the survey found scattered across families: the [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph) of learning systems, the [files-plus-git](#c/c-files-plus-git) curation of the LLM Wiki and Lean Blueprint, the [evidence-backed proposals](#c/c-edge-proposals) of SyllabusGraph and ACE, and the guided-graph UX of Understand-Anything. It follows from the finding that [no open-source project does all four pillars well](#c/c-claim-no-tool-does-all-four).

sections.heading: What is the opening?
sections.md: In the survey's words: a **local-first, git-backed concept DAG** where an agent *proposes* nodes and prerequisite edges with evidence and confidence, a human accepts or rejects them in a **review queue**, and learners explore a **zoomable graph with mastery overlays**. Nothing mature and open fills this slot.

sections.heading: Why is it open?
sections.md: Because each existing family covers only one or two of the four pillars. [Prerequisite systems](#c/c-prerequisite-graph-learning-systems) lack LLM co-authoring and good visuals; [AI tutors](#c/c-ai-tutors) lack a curatable graph; [code-graph tools](#c/c-graphs-that-teach-code) have the right UX for the wrong domain; [LLM curation](#c/c-llm-knowledge-curation) builds wikis and mind maps, not DAGs. The few projects that combine more, such as [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph), have almost no adoption.

sections.heading: Which existing ideas does it combine?
sections.md:
- **Curation and data format** from [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint): a typed dependency graph with per-node status, humans and AI in parallel.
- **Git-based content** from [roadmap.sh](#c/c-roadmap-sh) and Learn Anything: one markdown file per node, changes via PR.
- **Learner modeling** from [Oppia](#c/c-oppia) and [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder): prerequisite skills plus Bayesian Knowledge Tracing.
- **Evidence-backed extraction** from [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph): every edge cites a source, with an independent critic.
- **UX** from [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything): an LLM builds a graph, then gives a guided tour.

sections.heading: How would you start building it?
sections.md: The [suggested starting stack](#c/c-starting-stack): a folder of [concept files](#c/c-concept-files); proposer, critic and tutor agents; a React Flow [curation UI](#c/c-curation-ui) with an accept/reject queue; a [learner UI](#c/c-learner-ui) with a layered layout, mastery overlay and 'plan my path to X'; and [seed data](#c/c-seed-data) from Learning Commons or a user's corpus. The survey suggests shipping it as an [agent skill](#c/c-agent-skill-distribution) with a static viewer. The quick single-user version, the DIY PKM route, could get about 70% of the way in a weekend.

sections.heading: What are the risks?
sections.md: The survey flags several along the way. Prerequisite edges are where LLMs are weakest, so the product lives or dies on how cheap review is. Curation can still bottleneck if review needs experts for every edge, which is why ranking and reusing vetted graphs matter. Some promising building blocks carry license constraints, such as roadmap.sh's restrictive license and tldraw's commercial license for production. And the landscape moves fast: tools with tens of thousands of stars launched within months of the research date, so the slot may not stay open long.

concepts.title: Suggested starting stack
concepts.summary: Concept files, proposer/critic/tutor agents, a React Flow curation UI, a layered learner UI and seed data.
concepts.overview: The survey's suggested starting stack, if you were to build [the opening](#c/c-the-opening), has five parts. **Content**: a folder of [concept files](#c/c-concept-files) whose frontmatter holds requires, helps, objectives, sources, status and confidence. **Agents**: a [proposer](#c/c-proposer-agent) that extracts concepts and edges with citations, a [critic](#c/c-graph-reviewer-agent) that checks cycles, missing prerequisites and evidence, and a [tutor](#c/c-tutor-agent) for per-node explanations and quizzes. **Curation UI**: a [React Flow editor](#c/c-curation-ui) with an accept/reject queue, with git commits recording provenance. **Learner UI**: [Cytoscape.js or Sigma.js](#c/c-learner-ui) with a layered layout, a mastery overlay and 'plan my path to X'. **Seed data**: [Learning Commons or a user's corpus](#c/c-seed-data).

concepts.title: Learner UI
concepts.summary: Cytoscape.js or Sigma.js with a layered layout, a mastery overlay and 'plan my path to X'.
concepts.overview: The learner UI is the part of the [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack) that learners use. It's built on [Cytoscape.js](#c/c-cytoscape-js) or [Sigma.js](#c/c-sigma-js) with a [layered layout](#c/c-layered-layout) from dagre or ELK, a [mastery overlay](#c/c-mastery-overlay), and a 'plan my path to X' action that computes a [learning plan](#c/c-learning-plan) for a chosen target. It implements the survey's [DAG-first visualization](#c/c-dag-first-visualization): a layered view of one target's prerequisites, zoomable out to the whole field. Explanations for each node come from the separate [tutor agent](#c/c-tutor-agent).

concepts.title: Curation UI
concepts.summary: A React Flow editor with an accept/reject queue for proposed edges, recording provenance in git.
concepts.overview: The curation UI is where people review what agents propose. In the [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack) it's a [React Flow](#c/c-react-flow) editor, since the survey rates React Flow best for editable node-and-edge UIs, with an accept/reject [review queue](#c/c-review-queue) for proposed edges. Every decision becomes a git commit on the [concept files](#c/c-concept-files), so provenance, who approved what, is recorded by the repository itself. It's the practical form of the survey's fourth pillar, [human and LLM co-curation](#c/c-human-curation).

concepts.title: Concept files
concepts.summary: A folder of concepts/*.md files whose frontmatter holds prerequisites, status and confidence.
concepts.overview: Concept files are the content layer of the [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack): a folder of `concepts/*.md` files, one per concept. The markdown body holds the explanation; the frontmatter holds `requires` and `helps` (the [hard](#c/c-hard-prerequisite) and [soft](#c/c-soft-prerequisite) prerequisites), `objectives`, `sources`, `status: proposed|reviewed` and `confidence`. It's the survey's [plain-files-plus-git](#c/c-files-plus-git) recommendation made concrete, and close to what the [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/c-llm-wiki) already uses, plus typed prerequisites. Agents write proposals into these files; humans review them as diffs.

concepts.title: Seed data
concepts.summary: A starting graph: Learning Commons for K-12, or a user's corpus run through an ingestion pass.
concepts.overview: Seed data gives the graph a starting point so curators don't begin from nothing. The [suggested stack](#c/c-starting-stack) names two sources. For K-12, import [Learning Commons](#c/c-learning-commons-kg), a vetted prerequisite skeleton with an MCP server, following the advice to [reuse vetted graphs](#c/c-reuse-vetted-graphs). For anything else, run a user's corpus through a [LightRAG](#c/c-lightrag)- or [Graphify](#c/c-graphify)-style ingestion pass that finds candidate concepts, which is the job the survey assigns to GraphRAG-style tools. Either way, the proposer and the review queue turn the seed into curated prerequisites.

concepts.title: No open-source project does all four pillars well
concepts.summary: Every family of tools covers one or two of the four pillars; none covers all of them well.
concepts.overview: The survey's headline finding is that no open-source project today does all four pillars well: a [prerequisite model](#c/c-prerequisite-model), [visual exploration](#c/c-visual-graph), [LLM capabilities](#c/c-llm-agent-capabilities) and [human co-curation](#c/c-human-curation). Each family covers one or two. Prerequisite systems like [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy) have the data model but no LLM. AI tutors like [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor) have the LLM but no curatable graph. [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything) has the shape but only for code. [Co-STORM](#c/c-co-storm) co-curates, but a taxonomy. The closest, [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph), has almost no adoption. The gap is the survey's [opening](#c/c-the-opening).

sections.heading: What exactly is claimed?
sections.md: **No open-source project does all four well today.** The four are the survey's pillars: a concept graph with prerequisites, visual exploration, built-in LLM or agent capabilities, and human plus LLM co-curation. The space splits into groups that each cover one or two.

sections.heading: How does each family fall short?
sections.md:
- [Prerequisite-graph learning systems](#c/c-prerequisite-graph-learning-systems) have the right data model but little or no LLM co-authoring and weak visualization. [Metacademy](#c/c-metacademy) predates LLMs entirely.
- [AI tutors](#c/c-ai-tutors) have huge adoption but no explicit, curatable prerequisite graph. [DeepTutor](#c/c-deeptutor) uses graphs only inside retrieval.
- [Graphs that teach code](#c/c-graphs-that-teach-code) show the exact UX, but for codebases, where dependencies can be parsed. [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything) is the right shape in the wrong domain.
- [LLM knowledge curation](#c/c-llm-knowledge-curation) co-builds a wiki or mind-map hierarchy, not a prerequisite DAG. [Co-STORM](#c/c-co-storm)'s structure is a taxonomy.
- [GraphRAG infrastructure](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure) extracts entity graphs for retrieval and models no pedagogy.

sections.heading: What about the near misses?
sections.md: In the comparison matrix, [SyllabusGraph](#c/c-syllabusgraph) is strong on four criteria and partial on human curation (a human audit is still pending), and [PathFinder](#c/c-pathfinder) and [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint) come close too. But SyllabusGraph and PathFinder have 0–1★, and Lean Blueprint models proofs, not pedagogy. The DIY route, [Obsidian + Breadcrumbs](#c/c-obsidian-breadcrumbs) with the LLM Wiki pattern, reaches about 70% for a single user but lacks a learner view, mastery tracking and shared review. So the claim is best read as 'nothing *mature* does all four'.

sections.heading: What does it imply?
sections.md: It defines [the opening](#c/c-the-opening): a local-first, git-backed concept DAG where an agent proposes nodes and prerequisite edges with evidence and confidence, a human accepts or rejects them in a review queue, and learners explore a zoomable graph with mastery overlays. The survey says nothing mature and open fills this slot, and sketches a [starting stack](#c/c-starting-stack) for building it from existing parts.

sections.heading: How strong is the evidence?
sections.md: It rests on the survey's own review of a few dozen projects, scored against its rubric in the comparison matrix, not on an independent study. The scoring is qualitative (strong, partial, none), and some cells are judgment calls, such as Graphify's partial prerequisite model. Tools change fast: several entries are 2026 releases, and DeepTutor ships every few days. So the claim is a snapshot as of the research date, 24 September 2026, and should be rechecked before building.

concepts.title: LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges
concepts.summary: Frontier LLMs get prerequisite relations right only about half the time, so they need human checks.
concepts.overview: The survey's most important research claim is that LLMs alone are not reliable judges of prerequisites. The evidence is [K12-Bench](#c/c-k12-kgraph): on prerequisite reasoning, Gemini-3-Flash scores 57% and Gemma-4-31B 46% exact match. Since [prerequisite errors cost learners the most](#c/c-claim-prereq-errors-costly), this is why the survey insists on [human curation](#c/c-human-curation). Every AI-made edge should be a [proposal with confidence and evidence](#c/c-edge-proposals), uncertain ones go to a [review queue](#c/c-review-queue), and mastery should come from a [transparent model](#c/c-claim-transparent-mastery) rather than LLM judgment. [Few-shot examples](#c/c-claim-few-shot-helps) help, but don't close the gap.

sections.heading: What's the evidence?
sections.md: [K12-KGraph / K12-Bench](#c/c-k12-kgraph) (2026) built a curriculum-aligned knowledge graph and tested models on prerequisite reasoning. **Gemini-3-Flash scored 57% and Gemma-4-31B 46% exact match.** The paper's conclusion is the claim itself: LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges.

sections.heading: Why does it matter more for prerequisites than other edges?
sections.md: The design section says prerequisite edges are where LLMs are weakest *and* where errors cost the most. A missing or backwards prerequisite sends learners into material they can't yet follow. A wrong 'related to' link is noise; a wrong prerequisite is a broken lesson. Code tools avoid the problem because code dependencies can be extracted mechanically; general knowledge can't be parsed that way.

sections.heading: Can prompting fix it?
sections.md: Partly. The [MDPI study](#c/c-mdpi-llm-extraction) found that few-shot prompting beats zero-shot by about 6 points on relation extraction, and prerequisites gain the most from examples. Methods like [ProPRL](#c/c-proprl) aim at better prerequisite prediction. None of the cited work suggests the gap closes enough to remove human review.

sections.heading: What does the survey do about it?
sections.md: It builds the whole design around review. Make every edge a [proposal carrying confidence and cited evidence](#c/c-edge-proposals), the SyllabusGraph pattern; route low-confidence or high-impact edges to a [human review queue](#c/c-review-queue), the [ACE](#c/c-ace) pattern; record who approved what; and draw unreviewed AI edges in a distinct style. It applies the same caution to learners: [mastery should come from a transparent model](#c/c-claim-transparent-mastery), not LLM judgment.

sections.heading: Does this mean LLMs are useless for prerequisites?
sections.md: No. The survey's design gives LLMs the job they're good at: proposing many candidates quickly, each with its evidence, and ranking them by confidence. Humans then confirm the ones that matter, which [ACE](#c/c-ace) showed cuts expert effort a lot. Half-right proposals with citations are far cheaper to review than a blank page is to write, which is the difference between this and the [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck) that stopped Metacademy.

concepts.title: Prerequisite errors cost learners the most
concepts.summary: A missing or backwards prerequisite sends a learner into material they can't yet follow.
concepts.overview: The survey argues that prerequisite edges are not just where LLMs are weakest but where mistakes cost the most. A missing prerequisite drops a learner into a concept without its foundation; a backwards one teaches things in the wrong order. Either way, the learner hits material they can't yet follow and may blame themselves. Combined with the finding that [LLMs are unreliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges), this is why the survey sends such edges to a [human review queue](#c/c-review-queue), especially high-impact ones, and why it proposes [depth-qualified prerequisites](#c/c-depth-qualified-prerequisites) for precision.

concepts.title: Ranking candidate edges for expert review cuts effort and improves learning orders
concepts.summary: Having experts confirm only the top-ranked candidate edges saves effort and yields better learning orders.
concepts.overview: The survey's evidence that human-in-the-loop curation works comes from [ACE](#c/c-ace): it ranks candidate prerequisite edges, sends only the top ones to experts, and infers more from what they confirm. The result was a big cut in expert effort, and students who studied in ACE's resulting order had better success rates. The claim answers the [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck) directly: human review doesn't have to mean reviewing everything. It's the basis for the [review queue](#c/c-review-queue) at the centre of the survey's proposed design.

concepts.title: Plain files plus git beat a database for curation
concepts.summary: Curated knowledge works best as version-controlled files that agents and humans edit and review in diffs.
