concepts.overview: The survey observes that every successful curated-knowledge project it found keeps content in files under version control: [roadmap.sh](#c/c-roadmap-sh), [Learn Anything](#c/c-learn-anything), [Lean Blueprint](#c/c-lean-blueprint), the [LLM Wiki](#c/c-llm-wiki) and Understand-Anything's [committed JSON graph](#c/c-committed-json-graph). From that it claims plain files plus git beat a database for curation: agents and humans edit the same files, review happens in diffs or pull requests, and history comes free. It's a pattern drawn from examples rather than a measured result, and it underpins the recommended [plain-files-plus-git](#c/c-files-plus-git) design and the [concept files](#c/c-concept-files) in the starting stack.

concepts.title: Shipping as an agent skill drives adoption
concepts.summary: Graphify and Understand-Anything reached massive adoption by shipping as skills for coding agents.
concepts.overview: The survey attributes the massive adoption of [Graphify](#c/c-graphify) (~121k★) and [Understand-Anything](#c/c-understand-anything) (~84k★) to how they ship: as skills for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, rather than as standalone apps. A user already working in an agent can install the skill and get a graph of their folder immediately. From that it recommends [distributing a learning-graph tool the same way](#c/c-agent-skill-distribution): a 'curate a concept graph' skill or MCP server plus a static viewer. The evidence is two examples, so it's a strong hint rather than a proven cause.

concepts.title: Layered layouts beat force-directed for prerequisites
concepts.summary: For 'what do I need first?', a layered layout reads far better than a force-directed one.
concepts.overview: The survey asserts that because prerequisite graphs are [DAGs](#c/c-dag), not trees, a [layered (Sugiyama) layout](#c/c-layered-layout), with foundations at the bottom and goals at the top, reads far better than a [force-directed layout](#c/c-force-directed-layout) for the learner's question 'what do I need first?'. In a layered layout, direction is visible at a glance; in a force-directed one, it's hidden in arrowheads. The survey offers no study for it, but it shapes the recommended [DAG-first visualization](#c/c-dag-first-visualization) and the learner UI's dagre or ELK layout.

concepts.title: Few-shot examples improve LLM prerequisite extraction
concepts.summary: Few-shot prompting beats zero-shot by about 6 points, and prerequisite relations gain the most.
concepts.overview: The [MDPI study on LLM concept and relation extraction](#c/c-mdpi-llm-extraction) (2025) found that few-shot prompting, giving the model worked examples, beats zero-shot by about 6 points on relation extraction, and that prerequisite relations benefit most from examples. It's a practical lever for the [proposer agent](#c/c-proposer-agent) in the suggested stack. But it doesn't overturn the finding that [LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges); a few points still leave plenty for human review to catch.

concepts.title: Bottom-up concept graph construction beats top-down
concepts.summary: Building a concept graph from extracted concepts beat designing it top-down, in CourseMapper.
concepts.overview: [CourseMapper](#c/c-coursemapper), RWTH's MOOC platform, extracts concepts from course slides and links them to Wikipedia. Its authors found that bottom-up construction, starting from concepts extracted from the material, beat top-down construction from a designed hierarchy. The survey lists this among research worth knowing. It supports the pipeline shape of the suggested stack: ingest the sources, let a [proposer agent](#c/c-proposer-agent) extract concepts with citations, and let humans curate the structure that emerges.

concepts.title: Mastery should come from a transparent model, not LLM judgment
concepts.summary: Mastery should come from a transparent model like BKT or prerequisite credit, not an LLM's judgment.
concepts.overview: The survey's fourth design implication includes a rule for learners: mastery should come from a transparent model, [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/c-bkt) or Math Academy-style [credit that flows to prerequisites](#c/c-encompassing-edges), not from LLM judgment. The reasoning parallels the edge problem: if [LLMs are unreliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges), they're a shaky basis for deciding what a learner knows, and a transparent model lets anyone see why the system thinks a skill is mastered. It's part of [keeping the graph separate from the tutor](#c/c-separate-graph-from-tutor).

concepts.title: GraphRAG graphs are too noisy for teaching
concepts.summary: Entity/relation graphs don't model 'learn A before B' and are too noisy to teach from.
concepts.overview: The survey's verdict on [GraphRAG and agent-memory infrastructure](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure) is that its graphs don't model 'learn A before B' and are noisy for teaching. They extract entities and relations for retrieval, which is a different job from ordering concepts for a learner. The survey doesn't discard them: they could serve as the ingestion layer that finds candidate concepts in a corpus, which is how the suggested stack uses a LightRAG- or Graphify-style pass for [seed data](#c/c-seed-data). The pedagogy has to come from [prerequisite edges](#c/c-edge-proposals) reviewed by people.

concepts.title: The question: four pillars
concepts.summary: The four things an ideal open-source tool for learning with concept graphs would do.
concepts.overview: The survey starts from one question: which open-source tools already do most of what a learner-facing concept graph needs? It names four pillars. First, a [prerequisite model](#c/c-prerequisite-model): knowledge split into well-defined chunks, with edges that say 'you need A before B'. Second, [visual exploration](#c/c-visual-graph), so a learner sees where a concept sits, what it depends on and what it unlocks. Third, built-in [LLM and agent capabilities](#c/c-llm-agent-capabilities) that generate nodes, propose edges, explain, tutor and check mastery. Fourth, [human and LLM co-curation](#c/c-human-curation), where a person reviews and approves what the model proposes, with provenance. The evaluation rubric adds [chunked nodes](#c/c-chunked-nodes), [learner state](#c/c-learner-state), adoption and license. Every tool in the survey is scored against these, and none clears all four.

concepts.title: Key ideas
concepts.summary: The graph, ordering, layout and mastery ideas the survey takes for granted.
concepts.overview: Much of the survey assumes a handful of ideas. A [knowledge graph](#c/c-knowledge-graph) links concepts by typed relations; a [prerequisite graph](#c/c-prerequisite-graph) restricts those relations to 'you need A before B' and should be a [directed acyclic graph](#c/c-dag), so that a [topological order](#c/c-topological-order) always exists. [Mastery tracking](#c/c-mastery-tracking), for example by [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/c-bkt), estimates what a learner already knows. [Retrieval-augmented generation](#c/c-rag) explains why so many AI tools build graphs for retrieval rather than teaching. And a [layered layout](#c/c-layered-layout) versus a [force-directed](#c/c-force-directed-layout) one decides whether a learner can read 'what do I need first?' off the screen.

concepts.title: Tools for learning with graphs
concepts.summary: The families of existing tools, each covering one or two of the four pillars.
concepts.overview: The survey sorts the landscape into families, and each covers only one or two of the four pillars. [Prerequisite-graph learning systems](#c/c-prerequisite-graph-learning-systems) have the right data model but little LLM help and weak visuals. [AI tutors and course generators](#c/c-ai-tutors) have huge adoption and strong LLMs but no curatable prerequisite graph. [Graphs that teach code](#c/c-graphs-that-teach-code) show the exact product shape, but only for codebases. [LLM knowledge curation](#c/c-llm-knowledge-curation) co-builds wikis and mind maps, not prerequisite DAGs. The [DIY PKM route](#c/c-pkm-graphs) gets most of the way for one user, [community roadmaps](#c/c-community-roadmaps) prove demand for clickable maps, and a few [closed-source products](#c/c-closed-source-references) serve as reference points. Together they support the claim that [no open-source project does all four well](#c/c-claim-no-tool-does-all-four).

concepts.title: Infrastructure and building blocks
concepts.summary: Graph extraction, visualization libraries and agent plumbing a builder could reuse.
concepts.overview: Beyond finished tools, the survey lists the parts a builder would assemble from. [GraphRAG infrastructure](#c/c-graphrag-infrastructure) extracts entity and relation graphs from text; it doesn't model pedagogy, but it could be the ingestion layer that finds candidate concepts in a corpus. [Visualization building blocks](#c/c-visualization-building-blocks) such as React Flow, Cytoscape.js and Sigma.js cover the editable curation view and the learner's map, with [dagre or ELK](#c/c-dagre-elk) for layered layouts. And the [MCP server](#c/c-mcp-server) is the plumbing that lets agents call datasets like Learning Commons directly, and a way to distribute a curation tool.

concepts.title: What the research says
concepts.summary: What papers and benchmarks say about LLMs, prerequisites and human review, and the claims they back.
concepts.overview: The survey's research section explains why its design leans so hard on human review. [K12-KGraph](#c/c-k12-kgraph) shows that frontier LLMs get prerequisite relations right only about half the time, so [LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges](#c/c-claim-llms-unreliable-prereq-judges). [ACE](#c/c-ace) shows the fix: rank candidate edges and have experts confirm only the top ones, which [cuts effort and improves learning orders](#c/c-claim-human-review-cuts-effort). Other work shows that [few-shot examples help](#c/c-claim-few-shot-helps) and that [bottom-up construction beats top-down](#c/c-claim-bottom-up-beats-top-down). The survey's own claims, that [no tool does all four pillars](#c/c-claim-no-tool-does-all-four) and that [files plus git beat a database](#c/c-claim-files-git-beats-db), rest on its tool review.

concepts.title: Design lessons
concepts.summary: The survey's seven lessons for building a curated, LLM-assisted learning graph.
concepts.overview: The survey closes with seven design implications. Treat prerequisite edges as [proposals with confidence and evidence](#c/c-edge-proposals) and route doubtful ones to human review, because that's where LLMs are weakest. [Distinguish edge types](#c/c-edge-types) such as hard and soft prerequisites. Keep content in [plain files plus git](#c/c-files-plus-git), with [CI checks](#c/c-ci-graph-checks). [Keep the graph separate from the tutor](#c/c-separate-graph-from-tutor). Make visualization [DAG-first](#c/c-dag-first-visualization). [Reuse vetted graphs](#c/c-reuse-vetted-graphs) where they exist. And [distribute as an agent skill or MCP server](#c/c-agent-skill-distribution). Behind all of them sits the [curation bottleneck](#c/c-curation-bottleneck) that stopped earlier systems, and the finding that LLMs can't be trusted with prerequisites alone.

concepts.title: What to build
concepts.summary: The gap no open-source tool fills yet, and a suggested stack for filling it.
concepts.overview: The survey ends with a recommendation. [The opening](#c/c-the-opening) is a local-first, git-backed concept DAG where an agent proposes nodes and prerequisite edges with evidence and confidence, a human accepts or rejects them in a review queue, and learners explore a zoomable graph with mastery overlays; nothing mature and open fills it. The [suggested starting stack](#c/c-starting-stack) shows how to assemble it from existing parts: [concept files](#c/c-concept-files) in git, proposer, critic and tutor agents, a React Flow [curation UI](#c/c-curation-ui), a layered [learner UI](#c/c-learner-ui), and [seed data](#c/c-seed-data) from Learning Commons or a user's own corpus.
